Backward Pass and Optimizers

A model reads a sentence and gets the next token wrong. How wrong: one number.
Training uses it to move each of 671B parameters: which way, and how far.

Three things: computing that number (the loss), turning it into 671B derivatives (backpropagation), sizing the step (gradient descent, optimizers). One chain, from one number to one update.

Everything above saves at inference time. This lecture is the other half: in training, none of the four escapes the same bill.

Topic 1 followed one token forward to the model's guess. Here, the guess is wrong. Now what?

The error becomes one number. Not a table, not a vector: one number.

Training is one job: turn that one number into which way and how far each of 671B parameters moves.

✋ Someone always asks: how can one number decide 671B things? Too little information.

The answer is the lecture's thread: the 671B directions aren't read out of the number but computed from it.

It lives in the network's structure and every intermediate forward-pass value. The loss is the start; the chain rule expands it into 671B pieces. Hence Section 2's point that activations can't be discarded: to expand, keep what the expansion uses.

Three things, along that chain:

  • ① Where the number comes from: computing the loss (1.0).
  • ② How one number becomes 671B derivatives: backpropagation (Section 1). The core: brute force takes 20,000 years; backprop adds just 2× the forward time.
  • ③ Given the gradients, how big a step: gradient descent, optimizers (Section 3).

Three things, one chain. One number at one end, 671B nudges at the other.

⛔ What this lecture skips, so you don't wait for it.

  • Whether it fits. Enough HBM? Biggest piece? How to save? A few numbers for scale, no more.
  • Splitting it across devices. Tensor parallelism, pipelining, ZeRO's three stages: all Topic 5.

⭐⭐⭐ Sections 2, 4, 5's detailed math and every collapsible block fall under these. A Topic 5 preview; skipping them costs none of the three.

Why draw the line here Methodology, not one of the three things; safe to skip

Backprop and gradient descent are principles, unchanged for decades. Whether it fits is a per-generation hardware fact. Mixed, principles seem to expire too.

📐 Setting first, so each number has a known regime.

Unless stated, numbers use DeepSeek-V3's real pretraining config: sequence length 4,096, global batch ramping 3,072 → 15,360 sequences.

V3's advertised 128K is two 1,000-step extension stages after pretraining; the 14.8T tokens ran at 4K. Every 128K here is labeled context extension and converted to 4K. A number without its setting is meaningless: criterion ③ of this lecture.

Section 1

One number → 671B derivatives: backpropagation

Backprop isn't “running it again.” It costs two things: ~2× the forward compute and, worse, piled-up activations that can't be dropped early.

📌 First, pin down “activation.” It appears 60+ times here and has three common meanings.

  • Always the first here: what the forward pass hasn't yet discarded: intermediate results (layer inputs, norm outputs, attention scores…). §2 tallies their HBM.
  • Not “active parameters.” Last lecture's “V3 activates 37B per token” means the MoE weights selected at this step, not intermediate results. We use that sense only for MoE dispatch, written “activated experts.”
  • Nor “activation function.” SwiGLU, GELU etc. are always called “activation function” in full.

“Activation” alone means the intermediate results the forward pass leaves for the backward pass.

First, the starting point: the chain runs backward from one number, the loss, which deserves two minutes.

1.0 First: what kind of number is the loss?

Everything here aims to shrink one number. Start with it.

Step 1 · The loss is “how surprised the model is”

The model reads the text so far and guesses the next token, giving every vocabulary token a probability. We reveal the answer and check only its probability.

📌 Softmax turns scores into probabilities: exponentiate (all positive), divide by the sum (adds to 1). Every later use means this, as does “weights sum to 1” in Topic 3's attention figure.

loss = −ln p (p = the model's probability for the correct token)

Step 1b · From logits to loss, and where the “wrong guesses” went

First, where logits come from, or the figure's “row of scores” won't explain why there are exactly 129,280.

Where does −ln p get its p? Two steps.

The last layer outputs a row of raw scores, the logits. Any sign, any range; not probabilities yet.

  • ① Exponentiate: all positive, gaps widened.
  • ② Divide by the sum: they add to exactly 1; now probabilities.
  • ③ Reveal the answer; take −ln of its p.

✋ First, what that 0.6964 means: it is not the loss on a training curve.

Same −ln p, but shrunk twice to fit the figure: a 5-token vocabulary and a single position.

Compare it with random guessing over the same vocabulary: for 5 tokens, −ln(1/5) = 1.61. So 0.6964 says only “a bit better than guessing,” not “already well trained.”

A training-log loss = the real 129,280-token vocabulary + an average over all positions in a batch. Its random-guess start, −ln(1/129,280) = 11.77, is the 1.0 ruler's top and step 0 of the curve.

⭐ A common trap: half of the loss's size comes from the vocabulary, not model quality. A bigger vocabulary raises the same model's loss, so losses across different vocabularies aren't directly comparable (use a tokenizer-independent measure like bits per byte).

Two properties: elegant and life-saving.

① Adding the same number to every logit changes no probability. Only differences matter; exponentiation turns differences into ratios.

② Never exponentiate directly: it overflows. Real logits hit tens or hundreds; e¹⁰² far exceeds fp32's max. So every implementation first subtracts the row max: by shift invariance, mathematically identical, numerically safe.

6.4's z-loss is the flip side: this defuses overflow after the fact; z-loss keeps scores small up front.

✋ Now the class question: “Why don't the wrong tokens enter the loss?”

They do, just not under their own names: they sit in the softmax denominator.

Correct answer's probability = its exponential ÷ the sum of all entries, a sum over every vocabulary token.
⇒ Panel Ⓒ proves it: raise one “wrong” score by 1, correct entry untouched, and loss goes 0.6964 → 0.9702.

In the gradient, all show up. Each wrong token gets +its probability: the more it holds, the harder it's pushed down. Row sum: exactly 0.

⭐ In one line: invisible in the loss formula, visible in the gradient, and training uses only the gradient.
📌 Deeper: full cross-entropy sums over the vocabulary; a one-hot label leaves one nonzero term. So “looking at only one” follows from one-hot; it isn't the definition. With soft labels (label smoothing, distillation), every term appears in the loss.

Why this formula: it makes sense.

  • Confident and right (p → 1): −ln 1 = 0, no penalty.
  • The correct token got almost nothing (p → 0): −ln p → ∞, a huge penalty.
  • The logarithm gives “1% → 2%” and “50% → 100%” the same reward: each doubles p and cuts the loss by ln 2.
  • The log's real gift: d(−ln p)/dp = −1/p. The lower the probability, the larger the gradient, so the worst mistakes get fixed first. A draft said “otherwise it keeps nudging what it's sure of.” That doesn't follow: linear 1−p has constant slope −1, treating “sure” and “clueless” identically. Backward.

📌 Formally: cross-entropy, or negative log-likelihood. Three names, one formula.

Step 2 · Perplexity comes first; the loss is its log

Drop the log for now. The model gave the correct answer 0.4. What penalty should it get?

Most natural: the reciprocal. 1 ÷ 0.4 = 2.5

2.5 means the model is as good as guessing blindly among 2.5 tokens. (With 2.5 equally likely options, each would get exactly 0.4.)

That reciprocal is perplexity: “1 ÷ your probability for the answer.” Nothing mysterious.

p for the answerPerplexity = 1/pReads as
0.81.25Almost certain
0.42.5Like guessing among 2–3 tokens
0.110Like guessing among 10 tokens
0.01100Badly confused

⛔ So why the −ln? Purely so thousands of positions can be summed.

A sequence has 4,096 positions, each with a probability, and probabilities multiply. 0.4 to the 4,096th power is 0 on a computer: it underflows.

The logarithm fixes this: ln(a×b) = ln a + ln b. It turns multiplication into addition: add, average, never underflow.

Expand ln(1/p) and you get −ln p. That is the whole story.

To read it, exponentiate back: eloss = perplexity = the geometric mean of all the 1/p.

📐 Check it: three positions get 0.4 / 0.5 / 0.2. Average ln(1/p), exponentiate: 2.92; the geometric mean of 1/p: also 2.92. Same number, two routes.

❓ An aside people get stuck on: why is log 1 = 0?

A log asks: from 1, how many doublings reach this number?

Double each step: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8. “The log of 8 is 3”: three steps.

How many steps from 1 to 1? Zero; you're already there. That is log 1 = 0.

One step back divides by 2, to 0.5, so log 0.5 = −1. Greater than 1 is positive, equal to 1 is zero, less than 1 is negative.

So the loss formula holds up at both ends:

  • Perfectly right, p = 1 → perplexity 1 → no steps from 1 to 1 → loss = 0. Zero penalty for a perfect answer, not rigged: log 1 = 0 gives it.
  • Wrong down to 1 in 10,000 → perplexity 10,000 → loss = 9.21. The wronger, the costlier, without limit.

Perplexity 100 → 10,000 is 100×; the loss 4.61 → 9.21 only doubles. The logarithm compresses “how many times bigger” into “how many steps.”

Convention: only the answer's probability counts

Each of 129,280 tokens has a probability. The loss uses one: the correct answer's.

The answer is “cat”; the model gives “cat” 0.4, so this position's loss is −ln 0.4. “dog,” “table,” “the”: all ignored.

Other 129,279 wasted? No: they vie for probability with the answer.

Probabilities always sum to 1. Zero-sum: others up, this one down. Absent from the formula, they decide how far the numerator's p is squeezed.

Precisely: don't mix the two levels (I once got this wrong in class). Probabilities have no “denominator”; they always sum to 1 (zero-sum). Softmax's internal denominator Σ exp(raw score) varies, but at the score level. “The denominator grew” implies the total changes. It doesn't. Measured: one score 1.0 → 3.5; total 1.000000 → 1.000000; the correct token squeezed 0.629 → 0.175.

Is “only one” a rule, or a consequence? A consequence.

The full formula doesn't pick one probability; it compares two distributions: the model's column vs. the reference.

The reference answer: 1 for the correct token, 0 for the other 129,279. This “a single 1, all else 0” encoding is called one-hot.

Expanded (a four-token toy example; the model gives cat 0.4, dog 0.35, table 0.15, the 0.10):

TokenRef. qModel p Term = −q × ln p
cat (right)10.400.9163
dog00.350: × 0, gone
table00.150: × 0, gone
the00.100: × 0, gone
Total0.9163 = −ln 0.4

So we don't “only look at one”: the other 129,279 terms are multiplied by 0 and vanish.

Hence “cross”-entropy: two distributions compared. Entropy compares one with itself. These are the two I mixed up in the confession below.

📌 People write the reference answer, so it needn't be 100%.

  • Label smoothing: correct token 91%, the other 9% spread around. Same prediction, cross-entropy 0.9163 → 0.9913: the other terms really take part.
  • Distillation: the reference is a large model's full column. Every token takes part: the small model learns “cat,” and also “dog is close, table is nowhere near.”

Pretraining almost always uses hard one-hot labels, so here “treat it as 100%” is accurate.

Worth more than the definition: a model can be confidently wrong.

Say a wrong token gets 80%, the correct one 1%.

The perplexity at this position = 1 ÷ 0.01 = 100. Yet it doesn't hesitate: 80% on one token. Decisively wrong.

So perplexity measures accuracy, not hesitation.

Confession: I taught this backward in class. I called perplexity the spread (entropy): another quantity. One distribution, “one token 90%, nine sharing 10%”: same entropy; loss 0.11 if the 90% token is right, else 4.50: 81× in perplexity. Entropy measures confidence; loss, correctness. Low entropy, high loss: possible.

loss

⛔ The top row isn't a made-up value.

A freshly initialized model gives every token the same probability, p = 1 / 129,280. Plug it in:

loss = −ln(1 / 129,280) = ln 129,280 = 11.77

Its perplexity is exactly 129,280, the whole vocabulary: the definition of random guessing.

So the ruler's top is computed, not estimated, and moves with vocabulary size (129,280 checked in Topic 1). The bottom has no official V3 number: “around 2.0” is a rough public-model ballpark, a reference, not any model's measurement.

The bits column: yes/no questions needed to “pick” the token

Column two converts nats to bits (÷ ln 2). The conversion is trivial; the reading matters.

Bits count the yes/no questions needed to pick this token from the candidates. Each halves them: log₂ of the candidate count.

At init: the whole vocabulary, 16.98 questions. Late in training: 2.89.

The candidates shrink because of the context, not because the token got easier. Compressing 129,280 to an effective 7 is the forward pass's work; the 14.09 bits saved are that 17,500×.

⛔ Precisely: “an effective 7” doesn't mean 7 candidates remain; the vocabulary stays 129,280 and probability concentrates. It means: as hard as 7 equally likely candidates.

Expand: what shrinks the candidates; “an effective 7” as a picture Picture version of the text above: no context, the whole vocabulary; with context, a handful; the right panel shows “effective”

Mental math: memorize just two numbers.

ln 2 ≈ 0.693 (think 0.7) · ln 10 ≈ 2.303 (think 2.3)

  • Each 0.7 off the loss halves perplexity.
  • Each 2.3 off the loss cuts perplexity 10×.

Loss falls from 3.0 to 2.3: a drop of 0.7, so perplexity halved. No calculator needed.

Check the ruler yourself: from 11.77 down to 2.0 is a drop of 9.77; divide by 0.7 = 14 halvings; 2¹⁴ = 16,384×.
Exact: perplexity 129,280 → 7.39, a ratio of 17,496. 16,384 vs. 17,496: under 7% off; the magnitude is right.

Only the order of magnitude. Mid-run you never need two decimals; you need “is this normal?”

Why does it “get more expensive later”? The phrase recurs; settle it once here.

⛔ First, a smooth-sounding wrong explanation: “the log scale squashes the later part.” No. In ratio terms nothing changes: each 0.7 drop always halves perplexity, at 11 or at 2.

Two real reasons.

Loss drops 1PerplexityCandidates cut
11.77 → 10.77129,314 → 47,57281,742
6 → 5403 → 148255
3 → 220.1 → 7.412.7
2 → 17.4 → 2.74.7

① The absolute gain shrinks. A “drop of 1” cuts 80,000+ candidates early, near 2 fewer than 5, since few were left.

② The root: part of what's left is inherent in language. The next token really can be several things; no one, humans included, can call it.
Late on you're not learning but hitting a ceiling: that entropy is irreducible, never 0.

📌 Hence two models' losses compare only on the same dataset and tokenizer. Change the data and the ceiling changes.

This ruler returns in 3.5 (is the loss falling fast enough?), 6.1 (how big a jump is a spike?) and 6.3 (reading that table). Without it, all three are gut feeling.

Aside · nats, bits, perplexity: three faces of one quantity

The ruler used two terms, nat and perplexity. With bits, they are three readings of the same quantity.

Expand: nats / bits / perplexity on one two-sided ruler Conversion in the text below (1 nat = 1.4427 bits); this draws the ruler, with ticks

Nats and bits first: they differ only in the base.

A bit is the information in one binary choice (a coin flip's result); base 2.
A nat is the same with base e. The conversion is fixed: 1 nat = 1.4427 bits.

Why nats here? Only because the loss is defined with ln. With −log₂ p, everything would be identical, every number times 1.4427. A convention, not a deep choice.

Per token is from Step 3 below: each of a sequence's thousands of positions has a loss, averaged at the end. Full unit: “nats per token, on average.”

⛔ In bits, the number becomes tangible: a compression rate.

“Average bits the model needs to encode the next token.” A language model is fundamentally a compressor; the loss is its compression bill.

  • Random guessing: ln 129,280 = 11.77 nats = 16.98 bits. log₂ 129,280 is also exactly 16.98: picking one of 129,000 tokens takes 17 bits. Self-consistent, not a value someone typed in.
  • Converged: 2.0 nats = 2.89 bits.

From 17 bits to under 3: everything this model learned, as compression.

📌 Three faces; pick whichever fits:

  • nats/token: what the definition gives; what training logs print.
  • bits/token: compression; the most intuitive.
  • Perplexity: “hesitating among N tokens”; easiest for non-specialists.

They're identities, not three measurements: change one and the others follow. Don't cite them as three proofs.

Step 3 · One loss per token, averaged over a batch

So far, the loss at one position. In a 4K sequence every position predicts its next token, so one sequence has 4,095 losses.

⛔ It is 4,095, not 4,096: the last token has no “next” to predict. The 1 matters only as the denominator for the accounting in 1.2.

Average them all and you get this batch's loss.

“Average” is the root of much that follows.

The 1.2 figure's analogy: a room of people, each with a demand, averaged. The people: these tokens.

Batches exist first to avoid heeding one person, not to keep devices busy. This runs to Section 6 (not blowing up); math in 3.5b.

Step 4 · A single number, with units

Hundreds of billions of parameters in, one number out. No vector, no table: one number.

Remember this. 1.5 shows backprop is cheap entirely thanks to this “one”.

📐 Unit: nats/token (natural log). Section 3.3b uses it for the learning rate's units.

Expand: one number, or tens of millions? The grid draws it; this is the per-level count for self-checking. Skip when presenting

Almost everyone asks this once: “Why do you keep saying the loss is a single number? What I see is 129,280 numbers per token, 4,095 per sequence, and even more once you multiply by the batch.”

Everything you listed exists; it just isn't all called the loss. Two compressions sit in between.

LevelCountCalled
Token scores, one position129,280 logits / probabilities: not the loss
↓ First compression: keep only the correct answer's entry, take the negative log
One position's loss1−ln p
One sequence4,095One per position
One step (V3's global batch)62,899,200 (= 4,095 × 15,360 sequences)Still one per position
↓ Second compression: sum everything, divide by the number of valid tokens
Final loss1The point on your loss curve

Why compress it to one number? Not for looks.

“One number out” is what makes “one backward pass” possible.

Per 1.5, the seed goes on the right: one number, so you plant it once.
With 4,095 objectives you'd plant 4,095 seeds, one backward pass each. That is why multi-objective optimization costs more.

✋ Finally, an apparent contradiction:

“The loss is one number” and “the backward seed has over half a billion”: both true.

The loss as a quantity really is a scalar.
Differentiate it: one partial derivative per logit: every position × the whole vocabulary, ~530 million numbers (4,095 × 129,280; drawn in 1.2).

⭐ “How many numbers in the loss?” asks about the quantity; “in the seed?” about its derivative. One is 1; the other, over half a billion.

The lecture's job, in one sentence.

Move this number from 11.77 to ≈ 2.

That means knowing which way to nudge each parameter: this number's partial derivative for each of 671B parameters.

The problem: how to compute 671B derivatives?

1.1 The hard part isn't the derivative; it's 671B of them

Derivatives are high-school math. The hard part: 671B of them, fast, redone every step.

“High-school math” will lose some readers, so one figure covers the lecture's three words. No limits, no formulas: three sentences.

Expand: a real stage is not a scalar Above is a 1-D toy (one knob, one reading). A real stage is 7,000-odd dims in and out; its “slope” is a whole table. We never compute that table. Expand for details

The names explain it: derive, partial

A common mix-up: not deviation, but derivative. Deviation is departure from a reference (standard deviation), unrelated here. The term is partial derivative.

Derive is a picture: Latin dērīvāre = de (from) + rivus (stream): literally “to draw water off a stream”.

📌 Source: Etymonline (derive / derivative): Latin derivare “to lead or draw off (a stream of water) from its source,” from de rivo (de “from” + rivus “stream”); the math sense dates from the 1670s.

To derive is to draw something off. Today it suggests deduction, and the water picture is lost.

With that picture, both terms follow.

Derivative first.

A stream: input in, output out. A derivative asks not “what is it now?” but “move one notch, how far does the output move?”

Not a new stream: a second one drawn off this one. The first gives the output; the second, change per notch. One source, two streams.

Then the partial derivative (not deviation).

Now the input is 671B knobs. “Move the input one notch” breaks down: which knob?

The fix is blunt: free one knob, clamp the rest. Partial means “in part”: one variable at a time.

671B dimensions collapse to one: a partial derivative is an ordinary derivative again. Not harder: it cuts the hard problem into 671B ordinary ones.

First, brute force. Without it, backpropagation looks unremarkable.

⛔ Brute force (finite differences): nudge one parameter, rerun the whole forward pass, and see how far the loss moved.

671B parameters: 671B forward passes.

671e9 s ÷ 3.156e7 s/yr = 21,261 years (1 s per forward pass, already wildly optimistic)

That's one step of hundreds of thousands.

Backpropagation's real job isn't differentiating; it's collapsing 671B forward passes into one.

1.2 The seed: the first gradient

It starts from §1.0's loss. (Just one; that's the key to what follows.)

The first gradient? Take cross-entropy, the most common loss. The network outputs a distribution (next token “the” 0.3, “a” 0.2…); the answer is 1 in one slot, 0 elsewhere.

First gradient = guess − correct answer.

Too high: positive; too low: negative. It seeds the whole backward chain.

No coincidence: it is §1.0's −ln p differentiated once.

Differentiate with respect to the logits (not probabilities) and −ln p is exactly p − y: the model's probabilities minus the one-hot answer.

Back to §1.0: one −ln p, two derivatives, two results.

  • With respect to probability p: −1/p; lower probability, larger gradient. That's the motive: fix the worst mistakes first.
  • With respect to the logits: it reduces to p − y. That's the implementation: the seed is one subtraction.

One says “why move,” the other “how”: two faces of one loss.

So frameworks always fuse the two into one op: one step, not probabilities then derivative. Few losses are this pretty; this pair is today's default.

Precisely: that “subtraction” is the derivative with respect to the logits, not the probabilities (the pre-softmax output).
It matters: as the softmax step cancels, the gradient doesn't vanish where softmax saturates, half the reason softmax and cross-entropy always pair up.

Expand: a weight's gradient scales with upstream brightness Another question: which wire is cheapest to change? Forward answers it, not backward: root of 1.6's “can't discard activations.” Expand

1.2b Push the right one up, the wrong ones down: one move

✋ A revealing class question: does backward push the right one up and the others down, or just the right one, the rest a side effect?

Both, and it's one and the same move.

The seed, “guess − answer,” is a whole row, one slot per vocabulary token:
the correct slot: 0.40 − 1 = −0.60 (negative = push up); every other slot: its own probability − 0 (positive = push down). The 0.20 token gets exactly twice the push of the 0.10 one.

⭐ The row sums to exactly 0. Probability is conserved, so up and down are one redistribution. The other 120,000-plus tokens sit at probability ≈ 0, gradient ≈ 0: no share, no move.

⛔ Two conventions (the figure's “example” can mislead): ① 4,096 tokens give only 4,095 predictions: the last has no “next”; ② loss averages per token, not per sequence: the denominator: target positions actually scored, padding and packing boundaries masked (MaxText: total_weights; loss = xent_sum ÷ total_weights).

Ⓑ's arrows are easy to misread: a position's one arrow back is not “which way it pushes.”

Every vocabulary row pulls on a 7,168-dim vector; all 129,280 summed make that arrow: a net force, not a direction.

“Push up / down” applies only to one vocabulary slot (level Ⓐ); at “one position” it refers to nothing. So Ⓑ's arrows are neutral, not green or red.

⭐ How that net force is summed is all of §1.2c.

And “one backward pass per token, then average the 671B gradients”? Exactly the same result.

Differentiation is linear: averaging and differentiating commute. So implementations run backward once: not a shortcut, but equivalent and tens of millions of times cheaper.

⭐ The scalar is only a handle; backward doesn't start from it. It starts from a “position × full vocabulary” tensor, each entry “guess − answer” over the total. None of the 60-odd million positions' votes is erased at the loss; they add up later, in each layer's matmuls.

1.2c How one position's request becomes 671B numbers

⛔ A natural misconception that inverts the whole chain: different positions' 7,168-dim vectors can't be summed first.

The temptation: 4,095 positions, each a 7,168-long vector, so average them and pass the average back. Do that and the whole gradient is wrong.

Position i's blame pairs only with position i's input. The weight gradient multiplies each row by its own partner, then sums; summing the blame δ first pairs position 3's blame with position 900's input, a different quantity.

Summation does happen, on the weight gradient, not δ, once per layer. δ stays a “position × width” table; the position dimension survives to the end.

1.2d Settling up: where weight gradients are summed

⭐ Deeper: when does “settling up” happen? Asked in class: “Per function, or after the whole layer?”

Per function: each weighted op settles alone, independent of passing back.

Given δ, a weighted op does two things:
① Settle up: δ × this layer's input, summed over positions, updates this weight. Positions are consumed; nothing passes back.
② Pass back: δ × weight = the earlier layer's blame. Positions survive.

⭐⭐ These are 1.6's “two backward matmuls” behind training's 3× cost. One δ table, two contractions: one eats positions, one keeps.

⛔ Two common mistakes: ① The weight-gradient bucket is fixed-size: 4,000 positions just add 4,000 entries. Hence “one number per parameter,” not “one parameter set per token.”
② Layers add, never divide. The “÷ total” happened once, in the seed; dividing in all 61 layers would do it 61 times. Strictly a sum, not an average: the averaging is already in every entry.

As the class reasoned, a linear layer's weight gradient uses only same-position input; earlier tokens entered it via forward attention, not in backward.

Expand: settling up doesn't queue Minor here; key in Topic 5 · parallelism strategies: late layers finish settling while early ones still compute, and finished parts ship meanwhile: “hiding communication behind compute.” Expand to preview.

1.2e “Average”: how many levels?

How many levels does it have? Class guess: within a sequence, across local sequences, across micro-batches, across devices.

Layered, yes: three levels of addition + one division.

  • ① Within a sequence + across local sequences: one level. δ is “(local sequences × length) × width”; one weight-gradient matmul contracts it all.
  • ② Across micro-batches: gradient accumulation, one bucket, add only.
  • ③ Across devices (DP): all-reduce sums.
  • ④ Division: just once, by the global valid-token count.

⛔ Why not divide per level? That's an average of averages. Valid-token counts differ (padding, packing boundaries, the last batch). Divide separately and a small batch counts as much as a big one, with no error, no divergence, a normal loss curve.
Instead carry “loss sum” and “token count”; divide once at the end.

Expand: the source code; not my derivation MaxText's gradient accumulation does exactly this, line by line: sums, not averages; token count tracked separately; one division at the end, by the token total (not the micro-batch count).

1.3 The common snag: what flows back is not one number

Many picture one gradient value passed down. It isn't.

What flows back is a whole tensor, shaped exactly like this layer's output: each output position's share of the loss's blame. We call it δ.

⭐ Name δ, or the rest is jargon: δ is the activations' partial derivative.

δ is the loss's partial derivative with respect to this layer's output, the activation. So backward must differentiate by activations: layer k's weight gradient needs the loss's sensitivity to layer k's output, which only layer k+1 can send. δ is that chain.

But differentiating it isn't changing it, an easy confusion:

Take grad?Up­date?Then
WeightsYesYesSum across devices (÷ once, at end), to opti­mizer, 2 B/param
Activ­ationsYes (= δ)NoPassed back, freed after use, never billed

⭐ Activations aren't changed: they're not free variables. Inputs and weights determine them; only new weights change them, so optimizer state to “turn” them is pointless.

❓ δ is a full tensor too; why isn't it on 1.7's bill? It exists only at backward's current layer, freed after use. Activations live from forward to backward: 1.6's mountain. ⭐ Same size, one billed, one not: only lifetime differs.

⛔ A natural, misleading phrase: “activations are just a medium passing data along.” In forward, yes. But a mere medium would be dropped after forward, and they can't be: each layer pulls them out as input for its weight gradient. Better: forward passes activations; backward passes δ, and activations get pulled out to settle up.

Given δ from the next layer, a layer does two things (numbered as in the figure below; ① is forward):

  • ② Its weight gradient: δ × the input saved in forward.
  • ③ The δ to pass back: δ × its own weights.

One matmul each. One forward, two backward: hence 3× compute.

Counting isn't enough: unequal sizes would break 1 + 2 = 3. It holds because all three share one set of dimensions. For [B,in] × [in,out]: ① forward X·W, ② Xᵀ·dY, ③ dY·Wᵀ. Each is B × in × out, the same volume: exactly 3×. (Drawn to scale.)

The reason transfers: the last layer passes nothing back: drop ③, 2×. Frozen layers skip weight updates: drop ②, also 2× (3.8's LoRA). Memorizing “3×” answers neither.

Expand: what are the two “ᵀ”s? A transpose costs no compute (rows ↔ columns, no number changes, data often not even moved), and the shapes force it: dW must match W and dX X, so only a transpose fits. Expand for details.

The figure above has two ᵀs: Xᵀ and Wᵀ. Unpack it first, or the rest won't make sense.

① What it is: rows ↔ columns, no number changes

A 2-row, 3-column table becomes 3 rows and 2 columns after a transpose: the first row becomes the first column. No number is lost or changed; only the reading direction changes.

So a transpose costs no compute: implementations often move nothing, just read it differently.

② Why it's unavoidable: the shapes force it

Matrix multiplication has one hard rule: columns on the left must equal rows on the right. The multiply consumes the matching dimension.

Backward's two results have fixed shapes: dW must match W (so the optimizer can add it), dX must match X (so the previous layer can take it).

ArrangementConsumed dim.Why forced
① Forward X[T×d_in] · W[d_in×d_out] = Y[T×d_out] d_inOriginal: mix the input by the weights
② Weight gradient Xᵀ[d_in×T] · dY[T×d_out] = dW[d_in×d_out] T (positions)Only way to get d_in×d_out
③ Pass back dY[T×d_out] · Wᵀ[d_out×d_in] = dX[T×d_in] d_outOnly way to get T×d_in

With the result shapes fixed, a transpose is the only fit. It isn't an extra operation; it's the answer to “how do these have to line up?”

Two sentences, in plain words

Forward asks “how is the input mixed into the output?” ③ reverses it: “how is the output's blame split back to the input?” Same W, read backward: Wᵀ.

In ②, Xᵀ does something else: it moves the position dimension to the middle so it gets consumed. Every position's opinion of this weight is summed here: exactly 1.2d's “settling up.” The position dimension vanishes, so this result isn't passed back.

⭐ The orange line (asked in class): ②'s Xᵀ isn't recomputed; it's ①'s forward input, saved. That line fully answers “why activations can't be discarded”: backward needs X for dW. The arrow follows the flow: ① saved → ② used.

1.3b Do wrong early guesses hurt later ones? Not in training

The class got it right: in training, earlier guesses never affect this position.

Each position's input is always the ground truth, not the model's last guess. This is teacher forcing.

⛔ But it isn't “looking things up one token at a time.”

Training computes Q / K / V and attention in one shot, all positions at once.
It's the biggest shape difference from inference, which alone goes token by token, each waiting for the last.

Strictly, “the K and V before me” is “before me and me”: the causal mask shows a position itself, not later ones.

✋ So what's the cost? Exposure bias.

Training never shows the model its own mistakes; context is always right.
At inference it's all self-generated: one mistake and it's off its training distribution.

Hence long generations drift ever further. The model didn't get dumber; it's in untrained territory.

Why do it? ① Parallelism: self-fed, position t waits for t−1; 4,096 tokens means 4,000+ serial steps, impossibly slow. ② No early divergence: early guesses are awful; feeding them back blows up in one step.
A known cost that pays off.

📌 Sources (looked up): teacher forcing, coined by Williams & Zipser (1989) for RNNs; scheduled sampling (randomly feeding in the model's own predictions, against exposure bias), Bengio et al., arXiv 1506.03099 (2015). ⚠️ Today's large models still use near-pure teacher forcing.

1.4 Why partial derivatives make this easy

Because partials are local.

⛔ ❓ Most people object at once—and rightly.

“A weight reaches the loss through a whole matrix, not a scalar, and its effect depends on its layer's other parameters, which interact. Everything pulls on everything: how can that be computed?”

Both hold, and it's slightly worse:

  • Across a layer, effects add. Weights feeding one output are summed first.
  • Downstream, its effect depends on the other outputs. The next layer mixes them: “everything pulls on everything,” literally.

The magic: the whole tangle is compressed into two numbers.

A weight's gradient needs just two things (matmul ② of 1.3's backward pair):

  • the input it saw in the forward pass;
  • the backward blame at its output.

❓ Where did the cross-coupling go? Into the second number.

Not ignored: computed layer-wide at once, with the blame. The δ passed back already folds in everything downstream, cross-mixing too.

The complexity is real—but paid once per layer, not per parameter pair.

The price leads into 3.3b. Pairwise interactions are second derivatives, one per pair; at 671B parameters, unstorable. So we deliberately skip them and pay with small steps.
Nobody invented the learning rate: giving up second derivatives forced it on us.

An op's backward rule needs only “how I turn input into output,” not its neighbors or the network's shape.

Hence autodiff as a general-purpose library.

One backward for matmul, one for softmax, one for addition; the framework just chains them in reverse.

Nobody hand-derives the whole network.

The alternative is hopeless: a closed form for “loss w.r.t. a first-layer weight” expands through 61 layers into astronomically many terms.

The chain rule: never expand it. Just multiply 61 small local derivatives in order.

The two matmuls of 1.3 and the chain rule's “multiply” are the same thing.

In 1.2d, matmul ③ on the incoming δ is “multiply δ by my own weights,” passed on.

That multiply is a chain-rule link; “my own weights” are the local derivative.

So “61 local derivatives multiplied in order” is literal: matmul ③ done 61 times in backward. Matmul ② (weight gradient) is off the chain: each layer reads its value off it for the optimizer, passing nothing on.

“Gradient” now means two things: the weight gradient from matmul ② (all-reduced, optimizer input, 2 bytes per parameter) and the δ from matmul ③, the activation gradient (used once, on no bill). §1.8's all-reduce carries the first.

❓ And once multiplied together? The famous answer comes straight from the chain rule.

So how do deep networks train? Residuals: one plus sign

The diagnosis first. A gradient is a product of 61 local derivatives, hypersensitive to each term's average (two left rows above).

Both are just 10% from 1, half the previous ±20%, and collapse just as fully. No middle ground: decay or grow, exponentially. Closeness to 1 makes the point: if 10% per layer can't survive 61 layers, no care is enough. That's the whole reason deep networks wouldn't train before 2015.

A common misreading: “small gradient” ≠ “unimportant layer.” A gradient is effect per step; small means insensitive, so it must move farther for the same effect. It needs to move most. Yet parameter − learning rate × gradient gives it the smallest step. This inversion opens 3.3b and is the whole reason adaptive optimizers exist.

Mathematically, a residual turns y = F(x) into y = x + F(x).

Its local derivative goes from ∂F/∂x to 1 + ∂F/∂x.

Everything else follows.

  • The product gains an identity path. Expand the 61-layer ∏ (1 + ∂Fi/∂x): one term takes 1 from every bracket, and 161 = 1. For any weights, the gradient has a non-decaying path to any layer.
  • It swaps “multiply” for “add.” Without residuals, layer 3's gradient hinges on the product of layers 4–61; with them, contributions add: a bad layer adds one term less; it can't zero the path.
  • At init it is 1 by construction. F starts small (many codebases zero the last projection), so local derivatives start at 1 + tiny: effectively shallow, with F learned layer by layer.

“Residuals let models go deep” is no mystery: “some number” becomes “1 + some number”. 6.0's table blames both on local derivatives drifting from 1; residuals pin them near 1 structurally, and 6.5's tricks (Pre-LN, init scaling) tighten that screw.

📌 Source: He et al., arXiv 1512.03385 (ResNet). The same group's arXiv 1603.05027, “Identity Mappings in Deep Residual Networks,” has the cleaner identity-path derivation: one equation, the gradient reaching shallow layers through no weight matrix. Not expanded: “1 to the 61st is still 1” above is all of it.

1.4b Aside: what a second derivative is (not Adam's “second moment”)

Expand: second derivative vs. Adam's “second moment” Off the main line (a live question). A second derivative is the slope's rate of change (first: which way; second: how long the slope lasts). Optimal step = gradient ÷ second derivative: Newton's method. But it's N² numbers, 10 trillion devices for V3; skipping it isn't laziness. ⛔ Adam's “second moment” is unrelated: geometry vs. statistics; “second” is coincidence.

We just said “we deliberately don't compute second derivatives.” But what is one?

A second derivative is the slope's rate of change.

The first derivative (the gradient): “move one step, the loss moves this much”—the slope.
The second: “move one step, the slope changes this much”—pictured, how sharply it bends here.

First derivative: which way to go; second: how long this slope lasts. Two equally steep slopes, one soon flat, one never, need very different steps; the first derivative can't tell them apart.

Its use: the optimal step can be computed.

On a parabola, optimal step = gradient ÷ second derivative: one step down, no trial, no tuning.
It also cures 3.3b's “backwards” problem: turn sensitive knobs less, sluggish ones more; ÷ second derivative makes them comparable.

Cauchy's 1847 paper ends on this split: first order approaches from afar; second order closes in—this lecture's second half covers what to do when second order can't.

What is “Newton's method,” really? Built for solving equations, not optimization. 3 min; safe to skip

First, its original form: find the x where f equals zero. Guess a point, draw the tangent there, see where it crosses the horizontal axis, and jump there as the next guess. Repeat.

Replace the curve with its tangent. The curve is hard; the tangent is a line whose zero is obvious. Strikingly fast: typically each iteration about doubles the correct digits.

How did it become an optimizer? A minimum is where the derivative is zero.

Run root-finding Newton on the derivative: “subtract f/f′” becomes “subtract the derivative over its derivative.”

That is, gradient ÷ second derivative. So the “optimal step” above is not another formula; it is Newton's method itself.

An equivalent, equally exact, easier picture: Newton's method for optimization fits a parabola at your current point—matching the true curve in height, slope and curvature—and jumps straight to its bottom.
⇒ If the loss is a parabola, one step reaches the bottom—hence “one step to the bottom.”

Why not in deep learning? Two reasons, one computed above:

  • It can't be stored or solved. With many parameters the “second derivative” is N² numbers, and you must also invert it: N³.
  • And the loss surface is not a bowl. Near a saddle the table may be “curving up in some directions, down in others”—then Newton heads for the saddle, or even a peak. It only seeks zero derivative, valley or peak.

A middle road is quasi-Newton (the L-BFGS family): without building the table explicitly, it approximates its effect from recent gradients. Good in classical optimization, it never took off at huge scale plus mini-batch noise.

📌 Source (looked up): Newton had a similar method in the 1600s; today's iteration is Raphson's, 1690 (Analysis aequationum universalis); ⚠️ both then applied it only to polynomials.

⛔ Why not use it? Its size is the square of the parameter count.

With many parameters it is not a number but a table: one per parameter pair, the Hessian.

  • It can't be stored. The weights, 1.22 TiB, fit on 16 devices of 80 GiB; this table needs 10 trillion. Not a hundred thousand: ten trillion.
  • Nor can it be computed. Naive solving costs parameters cubed—at an exaFLOP/s, 9.6 billion years. The universe is 13.8 billion years old.

So “we deliberately don't compute second derivatives” isn't laziness—it was never possible.

⚠️ The “exaFLOP/s” machine is an arbitrary yardstick for magnitude only. Numbers computed in topic04-fig-second.py, pinned with asserts.

✋ Last, the easiest trap in the whole lecture:
Adam's “second moment” is not a “second derivative.”

Second derivative (Hessian)Second moment (Adam's de­nominator)
Of whatdiffer­entiate the parameters twice square the gradient, average
Yieldscurvature: how sharp the bend its gradient's usual size
Fieldgeometrystatistics
CountN squaredN

That both are called “second” is pure coincidence.

This is not pedantry; the warmup of 3.5 hinges on it:

Adam divides out “steepness,” not “curvature.”

The denominator is the gradient's root mean square, so however large this step's gradient, the update is pulled back to η's scale—“how steep” gets normalized away. But it never computes “how sharply it bends”: its N numbers don't hold that.

When you hit “Adam already handles the gradients; why still unstable?”—blame curvature, not steepness, and curvature isn't on Adam's books.

Likewise the “first moment” is not a first derivative but a moving average of the gradient; “first” means the statistical first moment (mean).

So why do people say “Adam's denominator estimates the second derivative”? Because a link can be drawn after the fact. But that's hindsight, not its inventors' thinking—see 3.3b, which starts from the problem each of three generations meant to fix.
⭐ The tell is size: Adam takes another road with 2N numbers, never aiming at that N² table. Hence “adaptive learning rate,” not “approximate Newton.”

1.5 The deepest point: why back to front

Expand: why back to front, not the reverse Off the main line: nobody asks about forward-mode gradients now. Right: one number, so one seeding pass. Left: hundreds of billions, so as many passes: at 1 s per pass, ~20,000 years apart (see 1.1). Expand for why one right-side seed suffices

In math, both directions work, same result. The only difference: how many passes along the chain.

The whole case for backpropagation, in one line: hundreds of billions of parameters, only one loss.

Many inputs, one output. If the loss were a million-dimensional output, not one number, this would no longer pay off; front to back would win.

So 1.1's answer: those 671B forward passes collapse into one backward pass.

This criterion transfers: whenever a problem needs many partial derivatives, first count inputs vs. outputs; that picks the starting end.

🕰️ Per public sources, it debuted in an unread master's thesis.

In 1970, University of Helsinki student Seppo Linnainmaa proposed reverse-mode automatic differentiation in his master's thesis: exactly this “push back from the output.”

And the thesis never once mentions neural networks. Pure math: efficiently differentiating a composite function.

Neural networks waited sixteen more years for the connection (the 1986 Nature paper).

We've seen this shape: 1.4's “vanishing gradient” also debuted in a master's thesis (1991, Munich, German, never in an English journal).
Twice, a game-changer debuted as an unread master's thesis.

How far each historical claim was checked

For 1970 I checked public biographies and surveys; I did not read the thesis (Finnish, not digitized): solid secondhand, hence “per public sources.”
For 1991 (Hochreiter's German thesis) I also didn't read the original, but the four-author 2001 survey is firsthand, one notch higher.
Cite neither as “I have read it.”

1.6 Closing the loop: backward reads forward values, so activations stay

In 1.2d, step ② (own weight gradient) needs “the input saved in the forward pass”: the activation.

⛔ The root reason activations stay: not bad design, but the backward math itself.

Every forward intermediate stays in memory until backward needs it; at the last layer, all are still there.

Both costs stand: compute 3× (forward 1 + backward 2); memory, every activation, first layer to last. Next: trade compute for memory.

📌 Ⓑ's two cards are one sequence, two configurations, not two models.

Both numbers are our own per-op derivation (V3 config + official reference MLA forward), no third-party check. Even if off by 2×, it still doesn't fit at this scale.

📌 How big is that “pile of intermediates”?

V3's real config, one 4K sequence: about 1.73 GiB per layer, 104.11 GiB over 61 layers.

V3's bf16 weights are 1,250 GiB; one sequence's activations, only about a twelfth.

But weights are fixed, while each extra sequence adds a full set of activations. At about 12 sequences activations match the weights; training batches always run well past a dozen. Hence the trade ahead.

❓ What's largest in that 1.73 GiB? It matters: Section 2 chooses what to drop.

Not attention. It's MoE's “nine copies.”

  • Expert outputs 28% + SwiGLU products 8%: one cause: each token goes to 9 experts (8 routed + 1 shared), each storing its own intermediates: nine copies. Together 37%, a layer's largest block.
  • ⚠️ Inputs don't count: the nine experts share one buffer (the upstream norm's output). Many implementations store a permuted copy for the grouped matmul (nine copies, 504 MiB at 4K); others redo the permutation in backward. An implementation choice, not a math necessity, so excluded.
  • Attention output: only 7%, a notch below most guesses.

This sets Section 2's list: save on the copies first, not attention. It also explains a paradox: MoE is cheap in parameters (each token touches few weights) but pays a nine-copy tax in activations.

Per-item counts and 128K figures: block below. “Does it fit?” territory, not required.

The activation bill, itemized: what a layer holds Safe to skip: for doing the math yourself (“does it fit?”)

1.7 The raw bill, itemized: what a layer actually holds

Optional. This is where the two numbers above come from, for readers who want to check the math.

First, the base unit: one hidden-width tensor = 4,096 × 7,168 × 2 B = 56 MiB. Every number below is a multiple of it. (Sequence 4,096, batch 1, bf16.)

Why 4,096 and not 128K: V3 was pretrained at 4K (all 14.8T tokens); 128K came after pretraining, via two 1,000-step extension stages. Every calculation here uses 4K; 128K appears only for comparison, labeled as context extension.

To convert: activations track only total tokens (see 5.1), so at 128K every number below is ×32 (131,072 ÷ 4,096). The one exception, the attention score matrix, scales with S²: ×1,024 (caveat 2 below).

What the MLA sublayer keeps

Norm output7,16856 MiB

❓ Why these tensors? One criterion: does the backward formula use it?

Frameworks store only what the backward pass will read. By op, the pattern is clean:

OpBackward needsStore?
Add y=a+b Derivative ≡ 1, needs nothingZero bytes

⭐ Additions are free; multiplies and nonlinearities aren't. Nets are nearly all the latter, hence dozens of copies per layer.

⚠️ A common misconception: “Adding a bias creates another activation.” The new buffer briefly appears and is freed after use; it never enters the “keep until backward” ledger, all the table records.

⭐ The table's biggest driver: not every copy is as wide as the input. Up-projected Q is 24,576 wide (3.4 copies); K/V, 32,768 wide (4.6 copies). So half of “dozens of copies” is width, not just count.

The “9 copies” deserve a pause, especially where they appear and where they don't.

9 = 8 activated routed experts + 1 shared expert. The nine copies are on the output side: each expert produces its own intermediates and output. The “expert outputs” item alone is 504 MiB.

⛔ The input side has no nine copies. All nine read the same memory: the “norm output” row above, already counted.
⚠️ In practice, tokens are often first permuted into contiguous per-expert blocks for grouped matmul. That buffer is a real copy: top-9 means each token appears nine times, 504 MiB at 4K. But some redo the permutation in backward instead of storing it: an implementation choice, so not in this required-tensor table. (Fixed live 2026-09-22: once counted as required, overstating by 448 MiB.)

On Topic 1's parameter-count table it is invisible. MoE is a bargain on parameters (each token selects only a small fraction of the weights), but pays a nine-copy tax on activations.

Altogether: one MoE block is about 1.73 GiB, one dense block about 1.24 GiB; 58 MoE + 3 dense ≈ 104.11 GiB.

📐 At the extension length (128K): ×32 ≈ 55.39 GiB per MoE block, ≈ 3331.39 GiB for the whole model.

Many remember this number, but it is the context-extension bill. For the 14.8T-token pretraining: 104.11 GiB.

⛔ Three caveats; state them whenever you present this table.

  • Derived op by op, not from a report. Frameworks vary widely in fusion, in quietly recomputing cheap ops, and in whether MoE dispatch truly makes 9 copies. Magnitudes only.
  • The attention score matrix is not included. It scales with S², the only item here not tracking the total token count. At 4K: 4.00 GiB per layer (128 heads × 4,096² × 2 B); at 128K: 4 TiB per layer (×1,024, not ×32). FlashAttention never writes it to memory, hence its absence. A naive non-flash implementation voids the whole table.

    Don't dismiss it as “only 4 GiB”: an entire MoE block's activations total just 1.73 GiB. This item alone outweighs it. At 128K it dominates; at 4K it is still the single largest tensor. The argument survives the new baseline: from “alarming” to “still number one.”

  • The 5.07 GiB peak is the bill “after the trade has already been made once.” It assumes each layer keeps only its input, plus the full activations of the layer being recomputed (3.34 GiB + 1.73 GiB), which is exactly recomputation. The second term is easy to miss: omit it and the peak is 34% low, memory ≈ a third short. It also assumes checkpoints sit exactly on layer boundaries and only one layer is recomputed at a time. Pipeline bubbles may hold more; the peak then scales with that count. The number holds only if both do. So raw bill first, Section 2 second: order matters.

One more item isn't in either table, because it belongs to no layer.

The final projection turns hidden states into scores over the vocabulary (logits), of shape [seq_len, vocab]. V3's vocabulary is 129,280:

4,096 × 129,280 × 2 B = 1,010 MiB (one 4K sequence)

Next to the two tables:

  • Largest in the tables: “K/V after up-projection,” 256 MiB.
  • Logits are 1,010 MiB, almost four times that.
  • A whole MLA sublayer totals just 722.5 MiB. Logits alone are bigger.

It is the model's largest single tensor, and softmax usually runs in fp32, doubling it again.

So real code almost never materializes it whole: they chunk the sequence: one chunk's loss, its backward, then the next. It is Section 2's recomputation idea, along the vocabulary dimension.

Mainstream implementations chunk it, so it is left out of the total above, deliberately. But write your own loop computing the full logits in one go, and this block suddenly appears in your memory: 31.6 GiB at the 128K context-extension length, and without chunking it won't run at all.

1.8 Gradient in hand, not done

1.3 stopped at the computed gradient. Several stages remain before it's used, none of them in inference.

Traffic size, and why batch doesn't change it Communication is parallelism: Topic 5

Stage ②'s traffic has a counterintuitive property

Pure data parallelism averages the full gradient across all devices every step. Its size: params × bytes per param.

The key: this traffic doesn't depend on batch at all. Feed one sequence or a thousand, and you send the same number of bytes.

Compute, meanwhile, grows linearly with batch. So:

the bigger the batch, the thinner this traffic is spread.

That explains two seemingly unrelated things:

  • Why large models keep raising batch size. GPT-3 ramped from 32K tokens to 3.2M, PaLM from 1M to 4M, V3 from 3,072 sequences to 15,360 (4K context, i.e. 12.6M → 62.9M tokens). All of them grow the batch as training goes on.
  • Why gradient accumulation saves more than memory. Updating once every K micro-batches divides all-reduces by K.

✋ Careful: a bigger batch does not buy throughput.

“Bigger batch is faster” has a precondition that fails at large scale: once parallelism saturates, per-step cost rises exactly as step count falls.

At this scale a bigger batch buys amortized communication and steadier gradients, not speed.

Curve and full trade-off: 3.5b, with two other folk sayings (“bigger is more stable,” “too big stops working”); the three go together.

Why the “can hide” lane matters

Overlapping compute and communication is a key training optimization. Inference has no counterpart: no backward pass, no long tail to hide transfers in.

Why clipping can't hide, and how per-layer clipping differs: see the figure's takeaway. Key point: the whole step's size is what links to 3.3.

Aside on ④: what gradient accumulation saves

  • Saves activations: one micro-batch's worth live at a time; the main win.
  • Saves traffic: one sync per K micro-batches.
  • Doesn't save resident memory: weights, gradients, optimizer state all intact.
  • Doesn't save compute: total FLOPs are unchanged.
  • May cost a bit more: accumulation runs in fp32 (see 3.2), so gradients go from 2 bytes to 4.

⭐⭐⭐ Gradient accumulation changes the timeline, not the total.

Scope: this stage exists, its size, whether it hides. Its form under other shardings (all-reduce or not) and volume: Topic 5.

“Parameters × bytes per parameter” is an order-of-magnitude convention: ring all-reduce goes out and back, about doubling traffic; MoE experts differ again.

Section 2

The cost: what can't be dropped, and the first real trade-off

The course's first real trade-off: not “is there a better way?” but “only one of two; which?”

In the core track because it follows from 1.6 (backward needs intermediates, so they can't be discarded). “Drop and recompute” is the next link, and its decision rule is valuable. How many GiB it saves and which level pays is a “does it fit?” question for Topic 5; details are collapsed.

2.1 Recomputation: store save points, not the whole run

Forward keeps every intermediate because backward needs it (1.6). Recomputation: don't.

When backward needs it, rerun the forward pass from this layer's input. Like a game save: keep a save point, not the whole playthrough, and replay from there.

2.2 Full recomputation: is the trade worth it?

The orders of magnitude to remember:

  • Saves: the activation block, the memory that grows with batch × sequence length. V3 at the 4K baseline: 104.11 GiB → 5.07 GiB, about 20.5×. The ratio is independent of sequence length (both sides scale together): 128K is also 20.5×, 3331.39 GiB → 162.14 GiB.
  • Costs: one extra forward pass; compute 3× → 4×, a third more.

So lopsided it hardly counts as a trade-off.

Large-model training turns it on by default. The question is how far, never whether (Ⓑ's three levels).

2.3 Selective recomputation: the rule is one number

Ask every intermediate one question: drop and recompute it in backward: how many FLOPs per byte saved?

Smaller ratio, better candidate; that alone yields the ranking.

For linear layers it has an elegant closed form:

A [S,k] × [k,n] matmul costs 2·S·k·n FLOPs to recompute and yields S·n·2 bytes (bf16). Divide: cost per byte = k.

The closed form assumes recomputation costs only the tensor's own op, true while its input is still there. Drop the upstream tensor too, and it must be recomputed first: cost accumulates along the chain, no longer one k. Our selective list keeps inputs present; watch this in your own.

Per byte, recomputing a linear layer's output costs exactly its input width in FLOPs. S and n cancel: independent of sequence length and output width.

So the best linear layer to recompute is the narrowest-input one; check the config.

Compare with 1.6: “biggest” and “most worth dropping” are two different rankings.

1.6 ranks by absolute size; this section by cost per byte saved, a ratio. No reason for them to agree.

Here they happen to agree: 1.6's two biggest items are both in the cheapest group.

  • SwiGLU products (8%): elementwise, cost per byte ≈ 0
  • Expert outputs (28%): input width 2,048, 2.20 TFLOP per GiB, under the “take all below 3” line

Luck, not a law. Counterexample, same table: the priciest item (o_proj output, 17.59 per GiB) is only 2.5% of a layer, little saved at high cost. On another model the rankings may conflict. Then choose by ratio, not size (cost per byte saved).

2.4 Attention breaks the pattern, and it must cross the linear layers

Attention isn't linear: cost grows with S², output only with S, so cost per byte grows linearly in S.

The figure's two lines, different slopes, are the whole section: one flat (linear layers, cost = input width), one climbing (attention). Different slopes must cross.

A constant and a climbing line must cross.

Compare against the widest linear layer. For V3: o_proj (projects the 128 concatenated heads into the residual stream), input width 128 × 128 = 16,384, not d_model's 7,168.

⛔ Why stress “not d_model”? I made that mistake first.

The crossover once read 5,734, using d_model (7,168) as “the widest linear layer.” Standard MHA has “heads × head dim = hidden,” so that works; MLA removes the constraint: V3 is 128 heads × 128 = 16,384, twice d_model.

The counterexample sat in the 1.7 table all along (“attention output 128 heads × 128 = 16,384”), half a section away, never cross-checked.

Rule: when the architecture changes, recheck any common-sense “A = B”. It raises no error; it skews every number downstream.

Hence: 1.25·S = 16,384 → S ≈ 13,107.

  • Below ~13K: attention isn't yet the priciest; dropping it isn't the layer's worst deal.
  • Above ~13K: past the widest linear layer, it stays priciest and grows linearly pricier.

13,107 is a rough crossover, not an engineering threshold: it hinges on causal halving, V3's head dims and the reference layer. Remember “different slopes must cross,” not the number.

Every tensor in a layer, ranked: the 9-row table, where to cut, save vs. pay Rule is above; this is the worked accounting (“does it fit?”)

Rank V3 at the 4K baseline: one MoE block, sorted ascending by TFLOP paid per GiB saved:

Don't memorize this table; it comes straight from the closed form above. Except the elementwise rows (cost ≈ 0) and attention (moves with S), each row's “paid/GiB” is just its input width in different units, so you can rank it from the config. A confession: one row was once hand-filled: “9.14 GiB saved × 7.70 per GiB” is 70 TFLOP, yet the column said 39.08. Yet the table's selling point is “you can rank it yourself”; anyone who did would have hit it. Now it's all generated; no hand edits.

⛔ “Is there anything that takes little memory but lots of compute?” Yes, attention. But how extreme it is depends entirely on the sequence length.

One criterion, a ratio: keep high, drop low. Here only the attention row moves with sequence length; the rest are input widths, independent of S.

Attention, paid/GiB4K (our baseline) 128K (extension)
Absolute5.50175.92
vs. widest linear (o_proj, 17.59) only 31% of it10× pricier

VerdictMarginalNever

Same model, same rule: go from 4K to 128K and attention goes from “still behind two linear layers” to “10× more expensive than anything.”

Don't overstate it: at 4K attention's ratio is 5.50, above the “take everything below 3” line discussed below, so by our own cut it isn't in the “take” group. What changes is whether it's the extreme outlier, not whether to recompute it: the first is a fact; the second depends on where you cut.

❓ Where does “below 3” come from? I chose it; it isn't derived.

In the table, the expert-output row is 2.20 and the next row, attention output, is 5.50; 3 just sits in the gap. Put it at 2.5 or 5 and the result is identical.

What actually sets the line isn't in the table: your current exchange rate, what a GiB of memory is worth to you in TFLOP.
Memory nearly full: move it right (drop more, pay more compute); compute-bound: move it left.

So don't memorize 3 as a threshold. The table is sorted by ratio; you only decide where to cut. The ranking is objective; the cut is your setup's call.

Cutting at 3 (taking every ratio below it): per layer you save 1.19 GiB and pay 1.53 TFLOP. Per step (one layer, forward + backward = 3 passes = 16.4 TFLOP): 9.3% more compute for a recomputable-pool saving of 71%.

Full recomputation, on the same per-step basis, is “pay 33% more, remove 95%.” Selective is still 2.7× more cost-effective, hence worth its own setting.

At 128K these numbers look very different, and much better.

Same cut: “only 1.9% more for 71%”; vs. full recomputation, 13.1× the value: truly “an order of magnitude.”

Why: the numerator (recompute cost) ∝ S, the denominator (one step) at 128K is inflated by S² attention. Longer S, cheaper-looking recomputation. “1.9%” is a flattering long-context number; don't cite it at 4K.

The direction holds, though: selective clearly pays at both baselines. And full recomputation's “pay 33% for 95%” is scale-free: it depends only on running forward twice, not on S.

Tighter: with FlashAttention, attention's backward is 2.5×, not 2× More precise; no conclusion flips

⛔ One convention to tighten: attention's backward is 2.5×, not 2×.

1.3's “backward ≈ 2× forward” is exact for matmuls with weights. But this lecture assumes FlashAttention throughout (1.7, caveat ②), and to save memory it recomputes the attention scores in backward.

From the FlashAttention-2 paper: “To get the FLOPs of the backward pass, we multiply the forward pass FLOPs by 2.5 (since there are 2 matmuls in the forward pass and 5 matmuls in the backward pass, due to recomputation).” (arXiv 2307.08691 §4.1)

Another instance of this section's theme: the memory FlashAttention saves is paid for by recomputation inside FlashAttention itself. “No free lunch,” with a concrete price.

With this lecture's shares: at 128K attention is 82.1% of a layer's forward, so a step is 3.41×, not 3× (3× undercounts by 12%); at 4K it is only 12.5%, giving 3.06×: no real difference. The rest of this lecture keeps 3×, a deliberate simplification.

“Selective +9.3%” and “full +one-third” once had different denominators (a forward pass vs. a whole step), so weren't comparable. As 2.5 says, “before comparing such ratios across papers, check whether they halved for causal.” Both are now per step.

First-party evidence the rule (FLOPs per byte saved = the producing op's input width) isn't just theory.

DeepSeek-V3, plainly: they “recompute all RMSNorm operations and MLA up-projections during back-propagation,” because “with a minor overhead, this strategy significantly reduces memory requirements for storing activations.”

RMSNorm outputs and MLA up-projections are exactly this rule's two cheapest categories: elementwise ≈ 0; up-projection input widths only 512 / 1,536. Our own rule, their actual config: stronger evidence than more arithmetic.

📌 Source: arXiv 2412.19437 §3.2.3.

2.5 The same rule gave the opposite answer in 2022

The idea of “selective recomputation” comes from Korthikanti et al., Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models, arXiv 2205.05198 (2022-05).

Same criterion as 2.3: drop parts that “take up a considerable amount of memory but are not computationally expensive to recompute.”

But it chose attention: QKᵀ, softmax, softmax dropout, and attention over V. Payoff: GPT-3 saves 70% of activation memory for only 2.7% extra compute; MT-NLG saves 65% for 1.6%.

Why reversed? Its sequence length is 2,048.

But use GPT-3's own slope: standard MHA, qk = v = 128, slope 1.00 (not V3's 1.25): 1.00 × 2048 = 2,048. GPT-3's widest linear layer is 49,152 (= 4h, the MLP down-projection's input width; V3: 16,384, o_proj's input width).

2,048 ≪ 49,152: far left of its own crossover. At 2K, attention really is the best to recompute. The paper was right.

Same rule, flipped conclusion. To be precise:

Not just sequence length. Slopes differ (1.00 vs. 1.25), as do reference layers (49,152 vs. 16,384): redraw both lines.

I got 49,152 wrong too: I first wrote 12,288, GPT-3's d_model. The rule needs the producing matmul's input width; the MLP down-projection's input is 4h. Same mistake on V3: I took d_model 7,168 as widest, missing o_proj's 16,384 input (128 heads × 128); the crossover was briefly wrong (fixed in 2.4). This panel's own point, and I stepped in it twice.

⭐ “Grabbing a relation that sounds like common sense” is the hardest error to catch.

No error, no blow-up; every downstream number just drifts. And since it sounds right, you've no reason to doubt it.

The same mistake, twice in this lecture: d_model as the widest linear layer, on V3 (missing o_proj's 16,384) and on GPT-3 (missing 4h's 49,152). One “common sense” rule, true on neither model.

What transfers is the shape, not the numbers. New model: redraw two lines, don't memorize numbers.

Another confession: this figure once applied V3's 1.25 to GPT-3 (2,560), in a lecture about “don't apply A's constants to B.” Rule: when two models share a figure, each line uses its own model's constants.

Mind the convention, or numbers won't match: the paper's 2.7% uses Megatron's classic formula, not halved for causal masking. In our causal convention, GPT-3's attention share is 1.37%. Both are right; before comparing such ratios across papers, check for causal halving.

Today this is handled for you. FlashAttention never stores the score matrix and recomputes it in backward: the paper's advice, built in.

In Megatron's source the default survives, with a maintainers' warning Fun, but a framework detail

⛔ I first wrote “so attention isn't even on modern frameworks' candidate lists.” Then I read the source. Exactly backwards.

Megatron-LM's selective-recomputation switch --recompute-modules: its first candidate, core_attn, is the default (recompute_modules = ["core_attn"]).

There are three layers here; I first covered only one.

  • ① “Default” doesn't mean “on by default.” recompute_granularity defaults to None: nothing is recomputed. core_attn is the default module once you enable selective.
  • ② With FlashAttention / fused attention, recomputing it is nearly pointless. The scores are never stored; what never materialized can't be “dropped and recomputed”.
  • ③ Most interesting: Megatron knows this, and wrote the warning into its source.

“If you are using transformer_engine as the transformer implementation, the core_attn is from transformer_engine and may be the fused version. For fused attention, you have no need to set 'core_attn' to recompute. Please check that the core_attn recompute is really needed.”

📌 transformer_config.py has if "core_attn" in self.recompute_modules: warnings.warn(...) (main, 2026-09).

So this isn't “a stale default nobody looks after”: someone noticed, left the default alone, and pinned a warning beside it.

Why not just change it? That's the interesting part.

Changing a default has a cost: results others got with the old one become irreproducible. Frameworks prefer a suboptimal default to voiding past results.

So the default becomes a fossil: it records the 2,048-era optimum. At that length it was right; at long context, by our table, it's the last to recompute; and under today's fused attention it has essentially nothing to do.

The lesson isn't whether to turn it on, but: for any default, ask what year it was picked and if its premises still hold. Me included: I first wrote “it's still the default,” collapsing three layers into one; readers would think it recomputes attention from step one.

The rest of the list matters more: layernorm, moe_act, mla_up_proj, i.e. RMSNorm outputs, SwiGLU products, K/V and Q up-projections, all cheap by 2.3's rule. All in the table's cheapest group. But not “exactly these, no others”: the list also has mlp / moe / shared_experts, and mlp is gate/up, the table's second-priciest row, far above the cut (the priciest is the o_proj output row). Our closed-form list matches the framework's options.

📌 megatron/core/transformer/transformer_config.py, field recompute_modules (main, 2026-09). Rule: before saying “modern frameworks don't do that anymore,” grep the framework. Such claims sound like common sense and go stale fastest.

Takeaway: backward needs intermediates, so they can't be dropped; but “drop and recompute” is a negotiable trade, settled by a rule you can derive, not by memorizing others' verdicts.

Beyond the three, folded below: recomputing can change results (random numbers, side effects, bitwise), and gains don't copy across scales (MFU / HFU).

Two off-the-books costs: results may differ; gains don't transfer Matters in practice, not for the principles of backprop, gradient descent or the loss

2.5b A cost off the books: recomputing may give other results

So far, two measurable costs. Recomputation has a third, in neither account, raising no error.

Recomputation assumes a forward rerun gives exactly the same result. Three things can break that.

① Random numbers: handled for you.

Forward has dropout. If recomputation draws a different mask, backward uses a different network. The gradient is wrong, with no error.

PyTorch is blunt: save the forward-time RNG state, restore it to recompute. torch.utils.checkpoint's preserve_rng_state defaults to True.

This also explains the third item on the checklist in 3.7: besides weights and optimizer state, a checkpoint must store the RNG state, for the same reason: random numbers are part of the training result, not transient runtime state.

② Side effects: nobody handles them.

Suppose the segment also modifies something on the side: updates a running statistic, increments a counter, writes a log line. Recomputation modifies it again.

The framework can't roll these back; it doesn't know what you changed. The rule: the recomputed segment should ideally be a pure function.

③ Bitwise mismatch: usually harmless, but it has one specific victim.

Run the same computation twice and the last bits may differ: reduction order or kernel choice is enough.

For training itself, differences this small barely matter. But they hinder bitwise reproducibility, exactly what PaLM achieved in 6.6 and what the “roll back + skip data” remedy in 6.2 presumes.

In short: recomputation closes the compute ↔ memory deal, but quietly demands reproducible results. The first two accounts say whether it pays; this one only shows when something breaks.

2.6 Takeaway: you can't copy others' gains

⛔ Same model, same switch, different scale: the gain can flip sign.

Why: recomputation shifts the compute-to-memory-traffic ratio, which varies anyway with parallelism and chip count.

A general rule (not only for remat): any parameter that changes shard shapes can't be copied across scales. Revalidate at the target scale.

2.5 shows the rule is harsher than it sounds: sequence length is on that list too, and it flips the gain's sign, not its size: the item most worth recomputing at 2K becomes the last to touch at 128K.

📌 Another number worth knowing, which you can compute:

Useful work is 3 units (forward 1 + backward 2); full recomputation adds 1, so 4 are executed. Recomputation is one-quarter of executed compute.

I originally wrote “one-third” here: that confused “one-third more than before” (1 ÷ 3) with “share of total executed” (1 ÷ 4). Same 1 unit, different denominator. 📌 The “one-third more” isn't our own derivation: the ZeRO paper says “33% re-computation overhead” verbatim (arXiv 1910.02054 §3.2).

That's why MFU looks so low: recomputation does real work, but by definition isn't in the numerator: not useful compute.

There are two metrics, differing by exactly the recomputation.

  • MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization): numerator: recomputation-free model FLOPs (the 6ND family).
  • HFU (Hardware FLOPs Utilization): numerator: FLOPs actually executed, recomputation included.

With full recomputation, HFU / MFU = 4 / 3: the “1 of every 4 units” above.

So for any MFU number, first ask which numerator it uses. Two papers' MFUs can differ by 30% just because only one used recomputation.

⛔ At long context, “low MFU” is not mainly due to recomputation.

Recomputation makes MFU at most 3/4 of HFU (a factor of 1.33). But 5.2 shows that at 128K, 6ND counts only 17.9% of the real compute; that convention gap alone is 5.6×.

⭐⭐⭐ The two factors swap places with sequence length: at 4K, 6ND undercounts by only 1.14×, so recomputation's 1.33× dominates; at 128K, the reverse.

In practice: at long context, turning off recomputation because “MFU is only 20%” recovers at most a quarter. First align the FLOP convention.

Section 3

With gradients, how big a step? Gradient descent and optimizers

Two sections fought activations. The biggest item on the bill has stayed silent.

3.1 How many bytes per param?

❓ One premise first; the bill below depends on it.

In training, each parameter sits in HBM twice:
① a compact copy (bf16, 2 bytes) for forward and backward;
② a precise copy (fp32, 4 bytes) for bookkeeping. Updates land here.

This is mixed precision. 3.2 explains why both are needed.

In mixed precision, each parameter carries five things; only the first is the model itself.

Remember one line: weights 2 bytes, optimizer 12.

“Optimizer state dominates HBM” isn't rhetoric. It's 2 : 12.

All 12 bytes are fp32; the next subsection explains why.

The 16 bytes: does mixed precision save resident memory? “Not one byte”: counterintuitive, pure accounting. Remember: Adam keeps two moments

⛔ A stubborn misconception: “Mixed precision halves memory, right?”

For resident memory, it saves not one byte. Add up both sides and you get 16 either way.

WeightsGradsMomentum m2nd moment vMaster weightsTotal
Pure fp324444—16 B
Mixed precision2244416 B

Look at that column: weights and gradients save 2 bytes each, but the master copy costs 4; the 4 eats 2 + 2.

So what does it buy? Two things, neither resident memory.

  • Speed (the main point). Matmuls run in bf16 on the chip's dedicated matrix units.
  • Activations. Stored in bf16: here you really save half. Per 5.4's toy example, often above resident state.

Rule of thumb: before saying “it saves memory,” ask which memory. Resident state, activations: two accounts. “Saves half” merges them and fails when it matters (e.g., will it fit one device?).

3.2 What needs high precision? One test: does it accumulate?

Why three fp32 boxes and two bf16? Don't memorize. One picture explains it.

The 12 fp32 bytes are exactly what keeps old contributions; the two bf16 items are used once and dropped. Not a coincidence: one test draws the line.

❓ Can gradients be fp32? Yes, in some implementations.

Usually for gradient accumulation over micro-batches. In bf16, big values swallow small ones and precision drains within a few rounds, so many implementations keep an fp32 accumulator.

That column then costs 4 bytes: 16 becomes 18.

📌 Our 16 is the ZeRO paper's classic accounting: 2 bytes weights + 2 bytes gradients + 12 bytes for three fp32 copies, written 2Ψ + 2Ψ + KΨ = 16Ψ, K = 12. arXiv 1910.02054. Sourced, but a configuration, not a law; quote its assumptions.

A small correction: the paper's two 2-byte items are fp16 (2019's norm), not bf16. bf16 is standard now. Same bytes, same bill, but different formats (see “Does bf16 need loss scaling?” in 6.6).

⛔ A first-party counterexample sharpens the test.

DeepSeek-V3 keeps AdamW's two moments in bf16, “without incurring observable performance degradation,” but master weights and gradients in fp32, gradients precisely for accumulation.

Right idea, too coarse: not accumulation, but unbounded accumulation:

  • Master weights: tiny increments over 100,000 steps; old contributions stay forever. Truly unbounded: fp32.
  • Momentum m / second moment v: moving averages. Each step scales by a factor below 1, then mixes in the new value; old contributions decay. Not an accumulator, so bf16 copes. (If β₂ isn't too close to 1: the closer, the smaller each step's change, until bf16 rounds it away. V3 uses β₂ = 0.95; see PaLM's step-dependent β₂ in §3.6. Corrected 2026-09-25: caveat added.)
  • Gradients: normally single-use. Accumulated, they become an accumulator and go back to fp32.

Tightened test: do old contributions stay forever? Yes: fp32. Decaying or single-use: low precision suffices.

“Must be fp32” isn't absolute: some have dropped it.

Master weights need fp32 because round-to-nearest erases small updates. Stochastic rounding (round up with probability set by the remainder) recovers it in expectation over many steps.

Finer still: the killer is not accumulation but accumulation + rounding the same way every time. Remove that bias and bf16 master weights are viable.

Not recommended: it needs extra support; fp32 masters are cheap and easy. Shown because knowing why a rule holds tells you when it breaks.

📌 Source: DeepSeek-V3, arXiv 2412.19437 §3.3.3 (“Low-Precision Storage and Communication,” not recomputation §3.2.3).
