It confirms the list nearly item by item: “We adopt the BF16 data format instead of FP32 to track the first and second moments in the AdamW … optimizer, without incurring observable performance degradation. However, the master weights … and gradients (used for batch size accumulation) are still retained in FP32 …” Accumulation reason included. The 16-byte table is no law: V3's per-param bill differs.

The test outlives this lecture. Why fp8 training is hard is the same question: as precision drops, what can go lower, what must stay? Still accumulation. Another lecture.

3.3 Why following the gradient lowers the loss

First, whose idea was this? Cauchy, 1847

⭐ Gradient descent predates neural nets by over a century. Augustin-Louis Cauchy, 1847, French Academy: “General method for solving simultaneous equations”.

He wasn't optimizing; he was solving equations.

The standard method, elimination, had two flaws, Cauchy notes: it often fails outright; when it works, the last equation is hopelessly complex, even from simple ones.

⭐ So he swapped the problem: minimize a function instead.

The function must be non-negative. Merging equations takes one line: u² + v² + w² + … = 0. Squares can't be negative, so the sum is zero exactly when each is. “Solve” becomes “drive the sum to zero.”

⭐ The invention isn't calculus (Newton, Leibniz) but the reframing: “solve the equations” → “walk downhill.” Every model we train runs on it.

⭐ The paper ends: once close, switch to the linear (Newton's) method to finish fast. He knew each order's place: first order from afar, second to close. 3.3b's “why everyone must estimate the second derivative” is this split at hundreds of billions of parameters.

📌 Source: A.-L. Cauchy, Méthode générale pour la résolution des systèmes d’équations simultanées, Comptes Rendus Hebd. Séances Acad. Sci. 25, 536–538 (1847). The two flaws, the sum of squares and the Newton line paraphrase the paper (English translation).

671B partial derivatives in hand. Which way to move?

Nudge every parameter: loss changes by Σ nudge × partial derivative. For small enough steps this is derived, not a rule of thumb.

This section's one crack: “multiply and sum” isn't the partial-derivative definition (a single-variable limit) but a first-order approximation (total differential). It needs small steps: the problem for the rest of this subsection and all of 3.3b.

For loss to drop, the sum must be negative. Move each parameter against its partial derivative: every term, “negative × positive,” is negative.

“Follow the negative gradient and loss falls” is math, not folklore. Among equal-length steps, fastest: the flip side of “gradient = steepest ascent.”

⛔ How small is “small enough”? No answer.

A partial derivative is the slope where you stand; it promises nothing a meter away. Overstep and you land higher than you started.

Direction: settled. Step size: no answer. It occupies the rest of this subsection and 3.3b entirely.

That figure left an ugly line: your start picks your valley. Alarming in 1D. The next figure dismantles it.

Two cross-sections, but the shape is 3D. Let's rotate it.

❓ “Enough dimensions means no pits” is wrong by one word.

Four dimensions or a thousand: either can hold a deep, sealed pit. Nothing forbids it.

⭐ The truth: a pit both high and sealed is extremely rare in high dimensions. Sealed pits exist; sealed implies low.

Why does height go with sealedness? Sealing needs every direction curving up. Up high there are more ways down, much height left to lose. Near the bottom fewer remain, until none: only then a floor.

⭐⭐ So in high dimensions nearly every stall is at a pass. Floors aren't forbidden; they're all very low, and you're not there yet.

Not just reasoning: it was measured.

Train to zero gradient, then count: how many directions curve up?
The fraction never reached 1.

Wherever training stops, some directions still go down. Paths exist; the slope was too flat.

✋ So: “Don't more parameters make training harder?”

Memory and compute: yes. Getting stuck: the opposite. Two questions; don't merge into “big models are harder to train.”

⛔ But not stuck isn't fast. Near a pass the slope is flat, the gradient tiny; with steps “proportional to the slope,” it crawls for ages. Most optimizers ahead fix this.

📌 Dauphin et al., Identifying and attacking the saddle point problem in high-dimensional non-convex optimization (arXiv 1406.2572, NeurIPS 2014). Abstract: the usual view blames local minima far worse than the global one; they argue “a deeper and more profound difficulty originates from the proliferation of saddle points, not local minima, especially in high dimensional problems …”.

⛔ A plausible fabrication: “each direction curves up or down at even odds, so all d curve up with probability 2^(−d).” Curvature signs aren't independent: no basis. We stick to what holds by definition.

⭐ The second half is key: saddles sit in “high error plateaus” that “can dramatically slow down learning, and give the illusory impression of the existence of a local minimum”. The enemy: crawling, not sticking.

Left over: no sticking, but flat passes mean crawling. The next figure is a first answer.

Why momentum works: three mechanisms; the famous one matters least

⭐ The figure above, escaping a shallow pit, is real but the least used of the three—sealed pits are rare in high dimensions.

① Coasting across flats. Near zero gradient, inertia remains. It treats crawling, not sticking: the high error plateaus around saddles.

② Stop bouncing off valley walls. Its main job in real training, the only one at work daily: same signs add, opposite signs cancel.

Recall 3.3b's valley, steep one way, flat the other: zigzag across, inch along.

  • Across the steep direction the gradient flips sign each step—summed, signs cancel, the swing shrinks.
  • Along the flat one it keeps its sign—the sum rolls ever faster.

⭐ Momentum is a filter: it amplifies the direction you keep and damps the one you swing in. Deep-net loss surfaces are usually narrow valleys; it nearly always helps.

⭐ Polyak's 1964 paper: inertia leads to motion “along the bottom of the trough.” The heading above, written in 1964.

③ Smoothing noise. Small-batch gradients are noisy; a moving average smooths jitter for free.

❓ When doesn't it help? There's a computable ceiling.

Classical momentum (Polyak's; PyTorch's SGD momentum): velocity ← β × velocity + gradient. A constant gradient grows velocity to 1 ÷ (1 − β) times it.

βSteady-state gainMemory span (steps)
0.805×~5
0.90 (most common)10×~10
0.99100×~100

⭐ That is its whole budget. At β = 0.9 the step grows at most tenfold. Taller pit walls trap it.

So “sometimes it fails” isn't mystery or mistuning: finite kinetic energy, computable ceiling. It escapes above because that pit fits within tenfold.

⛔ Flip side: overshoot. Near the floor, inertia carries it past; it swings a few times, then settles. Not free: end wobbles buy no stops en route.

⚠️ Both are “momentum,” but Adam's doesn't amplify. Easy to confuse.

  • Classical momentum: v ← β×v + gradient; a constant gradient grows v to 1/(1−β)×. It buys speed.
  • Adam's first moment: m ← β×m + (1−β)×gradient: a normalized moving average; at constant gradient, m → the gradient: no amplification. It buys a stable direction, not speed.

⭐ Same name, two things: one stores kinetic energy, one removes jitter. Adam's step comes from 3.3b's 0.2, not β₁'s speed.

⭐ So “escapes local minima” is its least-used side. Its daily work: coasting across plateaus and not bouncing between valley walls.

These three figures settle the direction: negative gradient lowers loss; high dimensions rarely trap; inertia crosses flats. Left: how big a step?

3.3b How big a step? Start with a units problem

Direction is settled. Now: how far to step.

A line nearly everyone has written: param ← param − lr × grad

Before units: two knobs show this line is backwards

📐 First, back to 3.3's Cauchy, 1847.

His paper closes: once close, switch to the linear, or Newtonian, method to finish fast.

That splits the job: first order from afar, second order to close.

This section: when second order can't close it.

The units argument is rigorous but slow to see. Two knobs show the result first, in grade-school arithmetic.

Two knobs, A and B; current error 1,000.

  • A is sensitive: a notch moves the error 100.
  • B is sluggish: a notch moves it just 1.

❓ How many notches each to cancel 1,000?

A: 1,000 ÷ 100 = 10 notches. B: 1,000 ÷ 1 = 1,000 notches.

Turns scale inversely with sensitivity: few for sensitive, many for sluggish.

What does param ← param − lr × grad give? A moves η × 100, B moves η × 1—100 : 1.

⛔ You need 1 : 100; it gives 100 : 1. Not slightly off: exactly backwards.

The sensitive knob overshoots, oscillating. The sluggish one barely moves, short after thousands of steps. The slowest knob sets the pace.

The inverse rule assumes independent, locally linear directions; real valleys curve, couple. Intuition, not formula. The exact-step figure is rigorous.

This is 1.4's vanishing gradient, restated.

There, chained products shrank the first layers' gradient to 0.0016. Often misread: “early layers don't matter.” Backwards.

Small gradient = sluggish knob = farther to go. It needs to move most; SGD gives it the smallest steps.

Be precise, or the views clash. A middle layer scaling the signal by 0.5× halves the upstream gradient; what doubles is the distance needed for the same effect. Reciprocals: one fact, two faces.
Mixed, they contradict; our convention: gradient = effect per notch, not distance to move.

The same point in units: why there must be a conversion factor

The units don't match.

The gradient is loss change per parameter change: unit loss ÷ param (per 1.0, loss is in nats/token, so nats/token ÷ param). “Param” isn't physical; weights are dimensionless. The parameter's own scale is the unit; it's conserved, so the derivation holds. This is SGD; Adam's second-moment division puts updates on parameter scale, so its learning rate has other units (exact-step figure). You want a distance: in parameter units.

So something must convert: the learning rate. Its unit: param² ÷ loss, i.e. param² · token / nat.

Read the unit aloud: the learning rate is not a pure number. It bakes in parameter and loss scales; loss scale depends on vocabulary (1.0's scale tops out at ln V). New model, vocabulary or batch: retune.

Units exposed, SGD's root flaw shows

One learning rate for the whole network, yet gradient scales differ by orders of magnitude. Below: same valley and rule, different rates.

Adaptive methods come down to one idea

Ignore gradient size, keep direction: divide out each parameter's own scale.

❓ Why divide? An exact answer, small enough to check here.

⛔ First, a misleading, near-universal claim: “Adam's denominator estimates f″.”

It's hindsight, not the inventors' view, and can't explain why it excels on sparse data or why it turns cautious when unsure.

The real path started from statistics, not geometry.

How it was found: three generations, one problem each

① AdaGrad (2011): rare words never got learned.

They had text in mind, not neural nets. “The” appears millions of times, a technical term three times, yet the rare ones often say the most.

With one learning rate that term never learns: its gradient exists only on its few samples, zero elsewhere; common features set the pace.

⭐ So: give each parameter its own learning rate, bigger for the rarely seen.

How often seen? Sum its past squared gradients: large if everyday, small if rare. Then divide by the square root.

⛔ Not a word on curvature or second derivatives. Pure statistics. Provenance in 3.4: its starting point is TF-IDF, not curvature.

❓ So what exactly is the “second moment”?

Square, average, root: the gradient's RMS, i.e. this parameter's usual gradient size.

⭐ Not curvature: this knob's typical recent response size, the parameter's own ruler.

What does dividing do? Current over usual size: how big this one is versus normal, a dimensionless number.

⭐ Raw gradient 100 or 0.01: after dividing, all share one scale. That's “adaptive learning rate”: relative to its own usual size, not absolute.

The full picture: “moment” and its real geometry

First, “moment.” In statistics, first moment = mean, second = mean square. Adam's v is a moving average of squared gradients; nothing more to “second.”

A picky detail: it's uncentered. E[g²], not the variance (which subtracts the mean); Adam holds m, the mean, yet doesn't subtract it.

Not an oversight: it's the source of the “signal-to-noise ratio.” Constant gradient: m = √v, ratio 1, full step. Divide by variance and it blows up: a constant gradient's variance is 0. Unsubtracted, the ratio is bounded.

Geometry? There is one, just not the assumed one.

Picture the loss surface as a long, flat ellipsoid: gradients large in some directions, small in others. Adam rescales each axis by its typical gradient size until all directions compare.

Diagonal preconditioning, genuinely geometric—but it scales by how much a direction usually moves, not how sharply it curves.

So it fixes mismatched scales, not sharp curvature. 3.5's warmup hits exactly that limit.

⭐ Also: it scales the axes but never rotates them. Coupling between axes is out of reach. Muon and Shampoo later target that gap: neither scales per coordinate (3.4).

② RMSProp: the ruler goes stale.

AdaGrad's fatal flaw: the sum only grows; steps shrink until training stalls.

Hinton changed one thing: a moving average replaces the sum.

⭐ Why: a parameter's “typical gradient size” drifts. Large early, small late. All history as ruler = a stale ruler.

③ Adam: numerator and denominator didn't match.

RMSProp had a ruler (denominator), but the numerator was the raw, noisy gradient; averaging it too gives momentum.

⭐ Now both are recent statistics. Numerator: direction; denominator: scale.

The alignment brought a bonus. The paper calls this ratio a signal-to-noise ratio:

  • Gradient steady, one direction: numerator builds, denominator holds, ratio → 1, a full step;
  • Gradient jumpy, sign-flipping: numerator cancels, the squared denominator still grows. Step shrinks itself.

⭐ So it does two things: evens out sensitive and sluggish, and turns cautious when unsure. The second came free, undesigned.

⭐ Finally, both paths side by side: the real lesson.

Cauchy's path is geometric: curvature sets the step. Rigorous; too costly at hundreds of billions of params.

Adam's path is statistical: ignore terrain, read the parameter's own history (usual gradient size; is this one unusual?).

⭐ Both end up close from wholly different starts. Hence “adaptive learning rate,” not “approximate Newton method”.

The key step: Adam's update ≈ “momentum ÷ √(second moment),” so the units cancel.

📌 In full: m̂ / (√v̂ + ε); ε (typically 1e−8) guards against ÷0. Strictly, units cancel only at ε = 0; ε carries gradient units, the one leak in “independent of gradient scale.” Usually negligible, but for tiny gradients (e.g. deep-layer vanishing, 6.5) ε, not √v̂, is the denominator, and Adam degrades to plain SGD.

Adam divides out the gradient's units: the step becomes a constant, whatever the gradient scale.

⛔ The constant isn't 1. It's 0.2. My earlier error: cancelled units make it constant, not 1.

Measured, it holds at 0.2–0.3, the same across model sizes.

If the gradient is mostly noise, a too-neat closed form follows:
update RMS ≈ √[(1−β₁) / (1+β₁)]
β₁ = 0.9 gives 0.2294, matching the measurements.

📌 Source: Su Jianlin, “Why Is Adam's Update RMS 0.2?” kexue.fm/archives/11267 (Scientific Spaces, in Chinese). Simulation (pure Gaussian gradients: 0.225) and a mean-field approximation agree.

The formula has only β₁, no β₂. So the βs split: β₂ sets memory length, β₁ step size (more in 3.6).

So Adam's learning rate changes role: not a conversion factor, a multiplier on a constant. Each parameter moves 0.2 × lr per step. Hence easy tuning: decoupled from loss scale and gradient size, one coefficient fixed by β₁.

The 0.2 also settles “retune when switching optimizers?”

Any optimizer scaled to update RMS 0.2 inherits Adam's tuned learning rate and weight decay. Kimi K2's Adam → Muon move did this: RMS set to 0.2, all else copied.

📌 Same source (Su Jianlin). The units thread's most practical payoff: make a quantity constant and it becomes an interface.

🕰️ Aside: Adam's original (2014) convergence proof was shown wrong in 2018 (Reddi et al., ICLR 2018). Fix: AMSGrad. Everyone kept using Adam. Working isn't proven. Details below.

That stumble: the proof's flaw, AMSGrad, and why nobody switched

⛔ 🕰️ This “add one more thing” lineage has a rarely mentioned stumble.

The original Adam paper (2014) came with a convergence proof. In 2018, that proof was shown wrong.

Reddi, Kale and Kumar, “On the Convergence of Adam and Beyond” (ICLR 2018, arXiv 1904.09237). In the abstract's own words, they give “a simple convex optimization setting where Adam does not converge” and “describe the precise problems with the previous analysis of Adam algorithm.”

The root cause is the exponential moving average itself: v forgets old large gradients, so steps along some directions can fail to converge indefinitely. Their fix is AMSGrad: make v never decrease.

What happened next matters most: everyone kept using Adam.

AMSGrad barely helped in practice, so the “wrongly proven” algorithm is cited over 100,000 times and trained every large model today.

The lecture's core idea in miniature: working and proven are different things. Its running lesson: don't trust conclusions; check assumptions.

Muon goes one step further

The figure covers most. Three points it misses:

  • Not “another tuning trick.” Ⓒ shows SGD and Muon answer one problem, differing only in the ruler for “step size”.
  • It ties to 3.1's bill. No second moment: 16 bytes per parameter becomes 12.
  • Its compute is nearly free (Ⓓ). Transferable: find idle time, then use it.

Ⓐ's middle column: on a diagonal matrix Muon reduces to elementwise sign: the vector approach is a special case of the matrix one. Teaching them as two things inverts that.

Steps the formula omits but training takes

Between gradient and update: all-reduce average across devices → clip once by global norm (against rare huge gradients) → schedule's current learning rate → weight decay → then the update.

The gradient says which way; the optimizer, how far.

Decades of evolution answer one thing: who decides “how far”?

  • SGD: you decide, so go tune it.
  • AdaGrad / Adam: the gradient's own history of scale decides.
  • Muon: the matrix's geometry decides.

That's the whole thread.

3.4 New optimizer, new bill

An optimizer is a memory decision, not just a convergence one.

Muon's saving has two limits, both named by its author.

  • 2D parameters only. Scalars, vectors, the embedding, and the output head still use AdamW; the writeup says input and output layers work best with AdamW. So the model saves less than that quarter.

    ⚠️ This hides two kinds of exclusion: scalars and vectors are out in principle: orthogonalization needs a matrix with several singular directions; on a vector it degenerates to plain normalization.
    But the 2D embedding and output head could take Muon; AdamW stays because it tests better: an empirical exclusion, not a principled one.

  • Each step is slower (per the writeup). Not “faster and smaller”: it trades memory for per-step time.

No conflict with Ⓓ (“fits into idle time”): “slower” is direction, “idle time” magnitude (under 1% of FLOPs, per Muon's author). Magnitude is configuration-dependent: a chain of mutually dependent small matmuls, where few FLOPs ≠ short wall-clock. Measure on your setup.

The evidence is hard: Muon raised the NanoGPT speedrun record 35%; since then (as of his blog post), twelve records by seven people all use it. Match it with tuned AdamW and you'd retake the record. Nobody has.

Link to the last lecture: DeepSeek-V4 trained most modules with Muon, one of three major upgrades in its abstract (arXiv 2606.19348).

One line, not a menu: each generation treats the instability its predecessor left. Read it against the 6.0 failure-mode table; no memorizing.

  • SGD: direction, no memory. Bounces on steep directions, stalls on flat ones.
  • + Momentum: treats the bouncing. Averaging past gradients cancels opposing parts, adds aligned ones.
  • Adagrad / RMSProp: treat mismatched parameter scales. One shared learning rate, but gradients span orders of magnitude (the two trajectories in 3.3b). Fix: divide each step by its own gradient RMS.
  • Adam: combines both: first moment for direction, second for scale. Price: 8 extra bytes (3.1).
  • AdamW: treats a side effect. The second moment scales weight decay, weakening it on large-gradient parameters. The fix applies decay to the weights directly: the decoupled in the title, and essentially the paper's one contribution.
  • Muon: treats the update direction itself. Elementwise Adam lets a few directions dominate a matrix update; Muon orthogonalizes it so steps across directions even out.

New optimizer, new disease treated. The cost always lands in one place: extra bytes per parameter.

Aside: what weight decay is, and why it lives in the optimizer

Below: how decay is applied. What it is, we've only touched on. Three questions settle it.

① What it is, and why it differs from the textbook

Each step shrinks weights slightly toward zero.

Textbook reason: regularization, no memorizing via a few huge weights (from ridge regression).

⛔ That fails for LLM pretraining: a single pass over data ≫ parameters leaves almost no room to overfit.

Yet every config sets it, always to 0.1: weight_decay = 0.1 in all DeepSeek models (with β₁ 0.9 / β₂ 0.95 / clipping 1.0). So what does it do?

A 2017 paper spelled it out: with normalization, L2 barely regularizes. It sets weight scale, which sets the effective LR.

Why: scale a weight matrix feeding a Norm by 2× and the output is unchanged (the Norm undoes it). Length doesn't change the function, only how far a given step turns the direction. Longer weights, smaller angle: lower effective LR.

Weights grow during training; left alone, the effective LR drifts down. Weight decay pins the length. It is now a knob that steadies the effective LR more than a regularizer.

📌 van Laarhoven, arXiv 1706.05350 “L2 Regularization versus Batch and Weight Normalization.” ⚠️ That paper is from the BatchNorm era. The same scale invariance applies to RMSNorm, but that's our extrapolation beyond its experiments (the rule in 2.6).

② How: by multiplying, not subtracting

θ ← θ − η·λ·θ = θ·(1 − η·λ)

Each step multiplies by just under 1: exponential decay. Without gradients, weights would go to zero.

How gentle? V3's peak η = 2.2×10⁻⁴, λ = 0.1 → 2.2×10⁻⁵ shrink per step; 80% remains after 10,000 steps. Very light.

⚠️ A trap: the shrink factor contains the learning rate. Change the LR schedule and regularization strength changes too: one knob turned, two moved. Hence in 3.3b's “order of one step,” decay comes after reading the scheduled LR.

In practice decay usually skips biases and norm gains. For a specific model, check its config; don't copy blindly.

③ Why it's in the optimizer: originally, it wasn't

It began as a loss term, ½·λ·‖θ‖²; autodiff turns it into λθ in the gradient. It was part of “what you optimize.”

Why move it? In the loss, it runs the gradient's pipeline: momentum, second moment, denominator, every stage. We want uniform pull.

Only the update step skips the denominator, and the optimizer owns it.

It went from “what you optimize” to “how you step”: new owner, same formula.

⚠️ Cost: out of the loss, you can't claim to minimize “loss plus a regularizer.” You no longer optimize the loss you wrote. Criticized, but it won in practice.

❓ The “W” in AdamW, pictured

Weight decay nudges weights toward zero each step so they don't grow. The question is at which stage.

The old way (original Adam): mix it into the gradient. Add λθ to the gradient; both are subtracted anyway. But every later stage then hits it, √v division included.

Backwards, as two parameters show:

Both at 10√vDecay termNet shrink
Common: big gradi­entsLargeScaled down Barely pulled
Rare: tiny gradi­entsSmallScaled up Pulled hard

Both at 10 deserve equal restraint, yet get the reverse. We want “pull every weight back a little, uniformly,” not “penalize by gradient size.” The two got tangled.

AdamW's fix: decay skips the denominator. The gradient path is untouched; the update separately subtracts η·λ·θ. That's “decoupled”; W is for weight decay.

❓ Muon drops the second moment entirely. Who now treats mismatched scales?

The list owes this: Adagrad names the disease; Muon throws out the medicine.

Orthogonalization treats it at another level.

Orthogonalization equalizes the momentum matrix's singular values (how hard it pushes along each direction). Each direction's step then ignores its gradient size: scale is erased all the same.

Adam's vMuon's ortho­gonal­ization
Where it erasesPer element, each by its own Whole matrix, singular values → 1
ErasesIts own gradient scale Gaps between singular directions
Cross-axis coupling Out of reach (axis-aligned; 3.3b) Within reach: singular directions span axes

That's also the cost. Adam's v also flags a parameter acting oddly “lately”; drop v, lose that. Muon keeps momentum: smoothing stays, per-element adaptivity goes.

⚠️ Orthogonalization equalizes only between directions, not the overall step size. Hence Moonlight (below) adds an overall-size rule; and once Kimi K2 calibrated Muon's update RMS to 0.2 (Adam's constant), Adam's whole hyperparameter set carried over.

Built for one reason, kept for another

The lineage above is hindsight. Its inventors were thinking of something else.

📌 AdaGrad (2011): the motivation was sparse features, not stability.

The paper: “infrequently occurring features are highly informative and discriminative,” so they get high learning rates, frequent ones low; “each time an infrequent feature is seen, the learner should ‘take notice.’”

Say “the” appears millions of times, a technical term three times. Under one learning rate, the term never learns. AdaGrad: discount each parameter by its accumulated gradient.

📌 Duchi, Hazan, Singer, JMLR 2011 (preliminary version at COLT 2010). The paper opens with TF-IDF as motivation (“We use this old idea as a motivation”), search's rarer-words-matter-more rule: an old information-retrieval idea, not curvature; the theory came later, as a guarantee.

📌 Adam (2014): the “equalize the size of every step” explanation starts here.

§2.1: the “effective magnitude of the steps … [is] approximately bounded by the stepsize setting α,” a “trust region … beyond which the current gradient estimate does not provide sufficient information.”

Plainly: whatever the gradient, every step is about the same size. Small gradients get lifted, large ones pressed down. That's where 3.3b's “0.2” comes from.

The paper calls m̂/√v̂ the signal-to-noise ratio: the smaller the gradient vs. its noise, the nearer the step is to zero. 📌 Kingma & Ba, arXiv 1412.6980 (ICLR 2015). The middle generation, RMSProp, comes from Hinton's Coursera slides: no formal paper.

⛔ While we're at it: “SGD doesn't work” overstates it.

SGD + momentum still competes on vision; on LMs Adam wins systematically. The lineage lists diseases treated, not useless predecessors.

The lesson is the mismatch: AdaGrad was built so rare words get heard; three years later Adam reread it as “equalizing step sizes,” the only framing we use today.

Rule of thumb: why a method was invented and why it stuck often differ. Tell only the second; people assume inventors knew. Usually they didn't.

Three state-saving branches, each cutting different bytes of the 16

Each changes a different box of the 16 bytes. Bytes per 3.1's accounting:

MethodBox changedBytes per paramCost
AdamW (baseline)—2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16—
MuonDrops the second moment2 + 2 + 4 + 4 = 12 2D only; made up by ortho­gonal­ization
LionAlso first moment only2 + 2 + 4 + 4 = 12 Sign of the gradient only
AdafactorFactors v into a row + a column That copy ≈ 0; 8 total, no first moment Loses v's per-element info
8-bit AdamBoth quan­tized to 1 byte 2 + 2 + 4 + 1 + 1 = 10 New storage, same algorithm

Three different approaches: Muon and Lion drop the copy; Adafactor uses a cheaper representation; 8-bit stores the same thing in fewer bits. So 8-bit stacks with the first two, which exclude each other.

📌 8-bit Adam quantizes states in small independent blocks, with nonlinear quantization precise for large and small values alike. Reported: 32-bit results across tasks, hyperparameters unchanged; a two-line drop-in swap.

📌 Dettmers et al., arXiv 2110.02861 (ICLR 2022 spotlight).

But “same algorithm, different storage” isn't quite true: per the abstract, 32-bit parity needs three things together: block-wise and nonlinear quantization plus a “stable embedding layer.”

The third changes the architecture, not storage. LM input tokens are very uneven, so embedding gradients vary wildly: quantization's worst case.

Rule of thumb: for a “drop-in replacement,” count in the abstract what it changes. “Two lines” is for the caller.

Scaling Muon: two additions

3.3b gave Muon's idea; good ideas don't automatically scale. A 2025 paper added weight decay (absent originally; the AdamW entry's disease) and a separate overall update-size rule, since orthogonalization only equalizes across directions.

With both, it works out of the box. Its scaling laws report Muon at ~2× AdamW's compute efficiency (compute-optimal).

📌 arXiv 2502.16982 (Moonlight, 3B/16B MoE, 5.7T tokens). “∼2× computational efficiency” is the paper's scaling-law result, not ours. Per 2.6, re-verify at other scales. Unverified: whether Muon still needs fp32 master weights.

3.5 How to draw the LR schedule

First, a ruler: not the optimum, just whether you're way off.

Only three decisions: where it starts, how high it goes, how it comes down.

The shapes differ completely: GPT-3 slides down after warmup; V3 holds a long, flat plateau. Plateau or not is the camps' only disagreement (third decision). Each decision below has a public config to copy, not guess.

Phase 1 · Warmup: the popular explanation is wrong

Tutorials say: early Adam's second moment is under-sampled, so ease in.

⛔ A systematic 2024 study says plainly this is not the main reason.

Its finding: warmup's overwhelming benefit is tolerating a larger target learning rate, by moving the network to a better-conditioned region. It rebuts “too few samples” directly: preconditioned curvature starts high, as high at large batch.

So warmup's real value: a higher peak, and an easier-to-tune one (wider usable range).

📌 Source: Why Warmup the Learning Rate? Underlying Mechanisms and Improvements, arXiv 2406.09405 (NeurIPS 2024).

“Says plainly … not the main reason” overstates it. The paper's Limitations admit small experiments: a 4-layer Transformer with context 64, plus a WRN on CIFAR-10. Orders of magnitude below this lecture's scale.

So why can the peak go higher? Back to 1.4b's second derivative; otherwise “better-conditioned region” is a tautology.

Curvature, not you, sets the largest step

On a parabola, gradient descent diverges once the step exceeds 2 ÷ curvature. Not slower: each step overshoots further, and it flies off.

So local curvature caps the usable learning rate: higher curvature, smaller legal step.

The paper measured high preconditioned curvature early in training, so high your intended peak isn't legal. It's as high at large batch: their evidence against “too few samples,” since a bigger batch would fix estimation noise.

So warmup is concrete: run at a safe learning rate and let the network walk to lower curvature. Once curvature drops, the peak is legal.

Causality: the surface flattens; the network doesn't learn to tolerate big steps. Hence longer warmup buys almost nothing: once you're there, more steps barely lower curvature.

Three misconceptions, all from the false premise “danger = large gradients”

❓ “Starting at a 1-in-129,280 guess, aren't gradients huge?”

A large loss isn't a large gradient. The initial loss, ln 129,280 = 11.77, is big. But in 1.2b's figure the logits-layer gradient is p − y: every entry lies between −1 and 1, the vector's length at most √2. Vocabulary 129,280 or 1,000: no difference.

❓ “Doesn't Adam normalize the gradient? What's left to be large?”

Good question; it points at the answer. Adam divides momentum by the gradient's RMS; units cancel, the ratio is O(1). So step size ≈ the learning rate, nearly independent of the gradient.

So the danger isn't early large gradients. What's large is the ground's curvature, not your step.

Take a step η. On gentle terrain the slope barely changes. On sharp terrain the same step overshoots the bottom, landing higher on the far side; each next step flies further: the 2 ÷ curvature line, live.

1.4b's point: Adam divides out “steep,” not “curved”. Its second moment is a statistic; curvature, a second derivative, is geometry it never computes. “Preconditioned curvature” means curvature after Adam's rescaling. Still high after rescaling? That's exactly what was measured.

❓ “Hasn't the denominator just not built up yet?”

Adam guards against that with bias correction: both moments are divided by 1 − βt to offset the short early history. No “zero denominator.”

“Noisy early estimates, so ease in” is what the paper rejected. Evidence: curvature is as high at large batch, which would fix estimation noise.

Don't push this too far: it doesn't mean “curvature keeps falling, so the learning rate can keep rising.” The curve stops at the peak, then falls (Phases 2–3). Warmup gets you to the peak, no further.

A third explanation exists; its premise keeps it out of modern models. New angle: Adam changes what “vanishing gradients” means.

The third explanation in full Premise: Post-LN (6.5 explains). On Pre-LN it doesn't apply; skip to the table below

An Adam update, as the source writes it:

Δθ = −η · E[g] ⁄ √E[g²]

Top and bottom share units, so the ratio is O(1) and the update O(η). Unlike SGD, where step ∝ gradient: small gradient, small step.

With Adam, vanishing gradients stop meaning “can't learn”: while the gradient beats noise, updates stay O(1).

⛔ But “no longer stuck” isn't good news: it trades the problem for a worse one.

At noise-level gradients, top and bottom are both noise, and the ratio is still O(1).

⭐ Full-sized steps; only the direction is random.

SGD just stalls in this regime: ugly, but safe. Adam charges off in a random direction at full step size.

That's where the trouble starts. The source's reasoning (premise: real, marked vanishing gradients):

  1. No warmup: fast from the start. Later, more sensitive layers learn faster.
  2. But the later layers take the earlier layers' outputs as input, and the earlier layers haven't learned yet, so they race ahead on bad inputs.
  3. They soon hit a bad local optimum; learning slows; gradients reaching earlier layers weaken further.
  4. Gradients go bad, but Adam's step stays constant-order: constant-order random noise. Direction scrambles; layers break front to back.

Per the source, warmup “slows the later layers' learning and gives the earlier layers more time to optimize, so all layers optimize in step”.

One symptom to match against your logs: Post-LN without warmup, the loss settles near a constant, then later diverges to NaN.

But keep its premise attached, stated plainly by the source:

“This assumes vanishing gradients. For Pre Norm-like structures, with no notable vanishing, training often works without warmup.”

So each has its own slot; they don't compete.

ClaimPremiseStatus now
Second moment under-sampledNone stated Refuted by the 2024 systematic study
Lets the network take a larger peak LRGeneral case Holds, but tested only to 4 layers
Hold later layers until earlier ones catch up Clear vanishing gradients
(i.e., Post-LN)		 Holds, with an observable symptom

The question isn't “which is right” but “under what premise.” Pre-LN or Post-LN decides which applies. Modern LLMs are almost all Pre-LN (§6.5), so the second is more relevant; but on a Post-LN model showing “loss flat, then NaN,” it's the third.

📌 Source: Su Jianlin, “Notes on model optimization: why is BERT's initial standard deviation 0.02?” (in Chinese), kexue.fm/archives/8747. Both quotes are his (our translation). It is his own analysis, not peer-reviewed; we take it as a premised explanation, not a settled result.

An ironic confession: 2.6 set “re-verify across scales,” then I broke it here, writing “they disproved it” with no scale. Rules are easy to write, hard to apply to your own citations.

How long? GPT-3: the first 375M tokens (0.125% of 300B); V3: the first 2,000 steps. Too short to count as a hyperparameter.

Phase 2 · How high to peak: copy a ready-made table

GPT-3's Table 2.1 lists peak learning rate and batch for eight sizes: a free prior, no sweep:

📌 GPT-3 family (same data and recipe; only size varies):

  • 125M → 6.0×10⁻⁴, batch 0.5M tokens | 350M → 3.0×10⁻⁴, batch 0.5M | 760M → 2.5×10⁻⁴, batch 0.5M
  • 1.3B → 2.0×10⁻⁴, batch 1M | 2.7B → 1.6×10⁻⁴, batch 1M
  • 6.7B → 1.2×10⁻⁴, batch 2M | 13B → 1.0×10⁻⁴, batch 2M
  • 175B → 0.6×10⁻⁴, batch 3.2M

The pattern: bigger model, smaller learning rate, larger batch. Mildly: 1,400× in size moves the learning rate only 10× (6.0e-4 at 125M → 0.6e-4 at 175B).

The paper: “larger models can typically use a larger batch size, but require a smaller learning rate.” They set batch by the gradient noise scale.

Batch and learning rate change together here (see the section's end). GPT-3 also ramps batch linearly from 32K tokens to target over the first 4–12B tokens. 📌 Source: arXiv 2005.14165 Table 2.1, Appendix B; the smaller-LR line is §2.3.

“Bigger batch, higher learning rate” has a ceiling many people miss.

First, the two common rules:

  • Square-root scaling: n× batch, √n× learning rate. Goal: constant update noise (update covariance ∝ η²/B, so η ∝ √B).
  • OpenAI, via gradient noise scale Bnoise: η* ≈ ηmax /(1 + Bnoise/B). Monotonic and bounded: however big the batch, LR only approaches ηmax.

So “double the batch, double the learning rate” is wrong.

Stranger still: under Adam, past some batch size the optimal learning rate may fall (the surge phenomenon). Cause, premise, dispute: in the fold below. Main line: don't blindly extrapolate any scaling law.

The surge phenomenon: cause, premise, dispute A disputed, advanced result (Su Jianlin criticizes the paper's approximation). Main text needs only “don't blindly extrapolate”; safe to skip

Under Adam, stranger still: past some batch size, the optimal learning rate falls, not rises: the surge phenomenon.

⛔ Why would that happen? Intuitively: adaptive learning rates are themselves suboptimal.

Treat Adam roughly as sign(g): the larger the batch, the closer sign(g̃) gets to the true sign(g). But is sign(g) the best direction? Not necessarily, especially late in training.
At a moderate batch, a little noise corrects that for you; enlarge the batch, the noise goes, and so does the correction: lower the learning rate more cautiously.

But this has a premise; the author deliberately added a caveat:

“(Of course, one more restriction: β is always below 1. If βnoise ≥ 1, the optimal learning rate still rises monotonically with batch size.)”

Su Jianlin faults the paper: its “the surge almost always appears” rests on a strong approximation, not very scientific; his more reasonable one gives “even if the Hessian's off-diagonal terms aren't negligible, the surge need not appear”.

📌 Su Jianlin, “How should the learning rate change as batch size grows?” (in Chinese) kexue.fm/archives/10542; on “Surge Phenomenon in Optimal Learning Rate and Batch Size Scaling.” Quotes: his words (our translation). Same caveat (his own analysis, not peer-reviewed): we take the warning “don't blindly extrapolate,” not a formula.

An apparent modern outlier: DeepSeek-V3, a 671B MoE, peak 2.2×10⁻⁴: far larger than GPT-3 175B, yet nearly 4× the learning rate.

⛔ My first explanation, which the table refuted: “V3 activates only 37B per token, so treat it as 37B.” But 13B is 1.0×10⁻⁴ and 175B 0.6×10⁻⁴, so 37B should sit near 0.8; V3 is 2.2. The new yardstick only shrank the gap from 3.7× to 2.8×.

The real answer: these numbers aren't comparable.

  • Batch sizes differ by leagues. GPT-3 175B: 3.2M tokens; V3: 12.6M ramping to 62.9M, 20× apart. And learning rate and batch move together.
  • Shapes differ. GPT-3's cosine decays early; V3's WSD holds its peak through 10T tokens. “Peak” means different things on the two curves.
  • Even the parameters differ. Most MoE parameters see few tokens per step: an order of magnitude fewer updates than dense.

Rule: a trend holds only inside the controlled experiment that made it. GPT-3's table is a prior because its eight sizes share one recipe, one knob moving, which is also why it's no prior outside it.
Confession: I first papered over it with “active size, not total.” The most dangerous claim: sounds like common sense, happens to fit.

Phase 3 · How to decay: two schools, same endpoint

Old school · cosine (GPT-3 / Llama / Mistral): cosine decay to 10% of peak over 260B tokens, then held there.

New school · warmup-stable-decay (DeepSeek-V3 has this shape)

V3's curve: 2,000 steps of linear rise to 2.2×10⁻⁴ → held constant until 10T tokens before decaying → 4.3T tokens of cosine decay to 2.2×10⁻⁵ → of the final 500B tokens, the first 333B stay at 2.2×10⁻⁵ and the last 167B switch to 7.3×10⁻⁶.

📌 arXiv 2412.19437 §4.2; clipping norm 1.0; batch 3,072 → 15,360 in the first 469B tokens, then held. A systematic analysis: arXiv 2410.05192.

The schools differ not in convergence but in when each forces you to decide.

  • Cosine fixes total steps up front: the shape comes from total length, so training longer means redrawing it.
  • The new school lets you stop anywhere: the middle is flat; decide the decay later.

⭐ The choice: “can I say now how many tokens I'll train?” Yes: cosine is easier. No: the plateau is your escape hatch.

Both schools end on the same number: the dashed line across the figure.

Takeaway: three tuning rules

  • ① Don't guess. Start from a public config close in size and architecture; the table above and V3's report are a free prior.
  • ② Don't copy across scales. Per 3.3b, LR has units: a small-scale value needs a transferable parameterization or a quick re-check at target scale.
  • ③ Judge by two curves. Loss blows up or grad norm spikes: too high; loss crawls, grad norm on the floor: too low.
    “Slow” has an absolute scale (the ruler from 1.0): falling from 11.8 is a normal start; near 2, every 0.01 is expensive.

Gradient clipping is a seatbelt, not a knob. V3 uses 1.0. Clipping to tame a too-high learning rate masks the problem, not solves it.

⛔ Easiest to overlook: a learning rate alone means nothing.

Report it with batch size, schedule shape, and total tokens; change one and it no longer applies. The two configs above are copyable because they spell out all four.

3.5b How big a batch? Why bigger is steadier, and too big stops helping

3.5 ended: “a learning rate alone means nothing; report it with batch.” So what sets the batch?

Step 1 · Unpack “batch”: four knobs multiplied

“Batch” as one number misleads. A real run has four independent knobs:

KnobWhat it isRaising it
micro-batch
m		 Sequences per device per forward Activations grow (1.7's table ×m)
Grad accum
K		 Passes per update (1.8, stage ④) Activations unchanged: only one set ever live
DP degree
d		 Replicas, each fed its own data Activations thin out; each replica holds all 16 B resident
Sequence length
S		 Lecture baseline: 4,096 Activations ∝ total tokens (5.1)

global batch (tokens seen per update) = m × K × d × S

⛔ The link that's easiest to miss: raise TP and the global batch shrinks.

Devices are fixed, so every model-splitting dimension competes with DP:

d = total devices ÷ (TP × PP × CP)

Raise TP from 8 to 16 and the DP degree halves; all else unchanged, so does the global batch.

The formula shouldn't contain EP (I corrected this once). Megatron-Core has two DP sizes: data_parallel_size = world_size ÷ (TP × PP × CP) and expert_data_parallel_size = world_size ÷ (ETP × EP × PP). EP divides only the second: MoE reshuffles the same tokens across experts; the step sees no fewer. CP does sit in the denominator (missing before). 📌 megatron/core/parallel_state.py: model_size = TP × PP × CP × gtp_remat.

Batch changes, learning rate follows: the parallelism knob is wired to convergence. It only looks like model splitting.

“Same code, same data, new parallelism config, different loss curve”: this is why.

Step 2 · Why a bigger batch is steadier

The gradient, like the loss, averages each sample's opinion (1.0).

Recall the “averaging a roomful of people” figure (1.2).

8 people in the room, one extremist: he drags the average far.
800 people: his influence is diluted to almost nothing.

Gradient “jitter” shrinks roughly as 1/√B: 4× the batch, half the noise.

📐 Sample-mean result (standard error ∝ 1/√n, independent samples). It assumes rough independence; adjacent tokens aren't, so effective samples are fewer than tokens. Order of magnitude only.

Conversely, a small batch is pushed around by noise every step: fuzzy loss, jumpy grad norm; many Section 6 spikes are lit this way by a few bad samples.

Step 3 · Why not keep growing it?

If bigger is steadier, why not enormous? The next two points sound separate but are one.

Side one · Noise falls, but so does “payoff per sample.”

While the gradient is rough, more samples sharpen it: 2× batch ≈ half the steps. Once accurate, noise isn't the bottleneck: steps barely drop, compute doubles.

The turning point is the “critical batch size”; past it, compute buys sub-proportional progress.

It isn't fixed: it grows with model size and training progress. So real configs ramp the batch: V3 from 3,072 sequences to 15,360 (last subsection's table). The ramp follows the critical point up; not for speed.

❓ Does a ramping batch mean adding devices? No. What ramps is gradient accumulation.

Recall Step 1's product: global batch = micro-batch × grad accumulation K × DP degree × seq length. For 5×, raise K from 1 to 5. Not one device added.

⭐ Nor does memory grow: per the accumulation row, “activations unchanged: only one set ever live.” Accumulation just postpones the update.

So what's the cost? Same devices, same tokens per second; only the tokens accumulated per update change. Fewer updates, same total time.

⭐ Ramping costs neither devices nor time; it costs update frequency. That's why it pays: early, the critical batch is small and big batches waste; later it has grown, so fewer updates cost almost no sample efficiency, buying fewer all-reduces (smaller communication share) and less noise, more stability.

📌 Three sources for batch ramp-up: mechanism, practice, framework.

  • Mechanism: McCandlish et al., An Empirical Model of Large-Batch Training, arXiv 1812.06162 (OpenAI, 2018). The abstract: “We find that the noise scale increases as the loss decreases over a training run”; the theory offers “a rough model of the benefits of adaptive batch-size training.” Source of the growing critical batch.
  • Practice: DeepSeek-V3 (arXiv 2412.19437): “We employ a batch size scheduling strategy, where the batch size is gradually increased from 3072 to 15360 in the training of the first 469B tokens, and then keeps 15360 in the remaining training.” Yet V3 kept the same 2,048 GPUs.
  • Framework: Megatron-LM has a first-class flag --rampup-batch-size <start batch size> <batch size increment> <ramp-up samples>. Help-text example: 16 to 1024, linear, in 126 increments. It also wants --global-batch-size (the target), and never asks your device count.

⚠️ Assumptions: the V3 sentence is from the v2 main text (near §4.2); the Megatron flag lives in core_r0.9.0's arguments.py; on main it's now --step-batch-size-schedule: same mechanism, new name.

Side two · A bigger batch needs a higher LR, which has a ceiling.

Less noise warrants bigger steps, or the accuracy is wasted. 3.5's eight sizes look opposite (bigger batch, smaller LR) because scale pushes it down too.

But the learning rate can't rise forever: too far and the loss blows up (Section 6). The batch speedup is capped by that ceiling.

⛔ Together, the two sides are one constraint.

Go back to the formula from 3.5:

η* ≈ ηmax ⁄ (1 + Bnoise/B)

Side one's critical batch, quantified, is Bnoise (3.5's “they set batch size using the gradient noise scale”). Side two's ceiling has the same Bnoise in its denominator.

So both turning points coincide, with an easy anchor: at B = Bnoise, η* = half of ηmax: at the critical batch you've spent half your learning-rate budget. More batch only creeps toward the rest, never reaching it.

This box once said “two independent reasons.” Wrong. “Independent” suggests dodging one, say by raising the ceiling a bit. You can't: ηmax is the divergence threshold (3.3b's “2 ÷ curvature”), not a knob.

The two “contradictory” claims are segments of one curve.

Bigger batch
Stability ✅ Monotonic: noise ∝ 1/√B; no turning point
Sample efficiency Has a turning point: past the critical batch, returns diminish

Both right, one row each. Choosing a batch means sitting between: steady enough, not yet wasteful.

Step 3b · Checking a third folk claim

Above: “bigger is steadier,” “too big stops helping.” The most widespread third: “bigger is faster”.

This claim has a premise, and it breaks at your scale.

Left: true. Unsaturated devices: fewer steps, none costlier. Really faster.
⛔ Right: false. Saturated devices: costlier steps exactly cancel fewer steps.

Tens of billions of parameters on hundreds of devices sits almost all on the right. For you, a bigger batch buys stability and thinner communication, not speed.

The math for “thinner communication” is in 1.8: cross-device reduction doesn't grow with batch; compute does, linearly, so it thins out.

Step 4 · Two details that bite silently

⛔ ① Forget to divide by K when accumulating = K× the learning rate.

1.8's conclusion assumes you actually took the average.

Sum K micro-batch gradients, then divide by K. Forget it and the gradient is K× too large, same as K× the learning rate.

The symptom misleads: no errors, loss falls at first, then suddenly blows up, and you suspect data or initialization. It's a learning-rate problem in disguise.

② With variable lengths, per-token and per-sequence averages differ.

One batch may mix 4,096-token and 500-token sequences (padding excluded).

  • Per-token average: every valid token counts equally; long sequences, with more tokens, speak louder.
  • Per-sequence average: average within each sequence, then across; equal say per sequence, so short-sequence tokens weigh more.

They give different gradients, one line of code apart. Pretraining almost always averages per token; the point is knowing which you picked.

Left out: an acronym we couldn't make out Author's note for the record; safe to skip

The live session mentioned something like “TPS”: “when TP is too large, TPS gets very large.” But by Step 1's formula, raising TP lowers DP and shrinks the global batch; of three readings (tokens per step / TP size / tokens per sequence), none fits, so no guess; skeleton only. Rule: don't complete an acronym you couldn't hear; a wrong guess teaches a relation that doesn't exist.

Takeaway: batch size is capped by sample efficiency, not memory. Memory decides whether it fits, not whether it should.

3.6 The other two knobs: what β₁ and β₂ do

Two numbers remain: β₁ and β₂. Usually left at defaults, yet their meaning is clear.

In one line: β sets how long old terms live.

A moving average scales by β and adds the new value: window ~1/(1−β) steps.

  • β₁ = 0.9 → momentum window ~10 steps, enough to smooth directional jitter.
  • β₂ = 0.95 → about 20 steps; β₂ = 0.99 → about 100 steps.

Higher β₂: steadier denominator, slower reaction; lower: tighter tracking, more noise. No magic: a memory-length knob.

PaLM's twist: β₂ changes with the step

It uses β₂ = 1 − k−0.8, where k is the current step.

Plug in a few numbers:

  • Step 100: β₂ ≈ 0.975, window ~40 steps.
  • Step 10K: β₂ ≈ 0.9994, window ~1,600 steps.
  • Step 100K: β₂ ≈ 0.9999, window ~10K steps.

The window grows with training (roughly as k0.8). A fixed β₂ = 0.99 remembers only 100 steps throughout.

❓ Why? The paper's reason is concrete.

The culprit: rare embedding tokens, which may appear once in thousands of steps. In a 100-step window their second-moment estimate is garbage: mostly zero, occasionally large.

A window that grows with training fixes it. The paper: “We have found this to be more stable than the standard β2 = 0.99.”

📌 arXiv 2204.02311, hyperparameters; also β₁ = 0.9, LR 10⁻² for the first 10,000 steps, then 1/√k decay.

⭐ Pause: you've seen this reason once already.

AdaGrad (2011) was built for exactly 3.3b's reason: rare features don't get learned.

PaLM (2022), eleven years later via another door (β₂'s memory window), hit the same problem: rare tokens are too sparse for short-window statistics to be trusted.

One gives bigger steps, the other longer memory: two doors to one problem.

⛔ But they differ: AdaGrad changes the denominator's size (bigger steps for rare parameters); PaLM, its sampling window (so noise doesn't dominate their denominators). Same disease, different medicine.

This collides with the rule in 3.2.

3.2 said: momentum and second moment are moving averages, old contributions decay, so bf16 copes.
But at β₂ = 0.9999 the “decay” barely decays; v approaches a true accumulator.

So that rule needs a premise: β doesn't approach 1 over training. Our inference, not the paper's: PaLM uses an Adafactor-family optimizer and reports no precision config, so there's no evidence the effect shows up. A conjecture.

One more find: GPT-3's hand-tuned table, automated by PaLM

PaLM runs unfactorized Adafactor, per the paper “effectively equivalent to Adam with ‘parameter scaling’”: LR scaled by matrix RMS.

The tie to 3.5: “the effect of this is similar to the manual scaling down of Adam learning rate as in Brown et al. (2020)” (GPT-3).

3.5's eight configs are the manual fix; parameter scaling the automatic one. Bonus, per the paper: parameters with inherently different scales (embeddings, layer-norm scales) aren't scaled down at the same rate.

What a checkpoint stores; why 12 bytes Storage, not one of the three things

3.7 A checkpoint stores exactly those 12 bytes

This follows directly from the bill in 3.1; no documentation needed.

Of those 16 bytes, which must go into the checkpoint? Ask, slot by slot, “if it's lost, can it be rebuilt?”

  • bf16 weights (2 bytes): no need to store; one cast of the fp32 master rebuilds them.
  • bf16 gradients (2 bytes): no need to store. The next step recomputes them.
  • fp32 master weights (4 bytes): must be stored, and not just as bf16. Saving as bf16 throws away all the low-order bits accumulated so far.
  • Momentum m, second moment v (4 B each): must be stored. They're history: lost, they reset to zero.

So checkpoint size = those 12 bytes × parameter count. For 671B: about 7.3 TiB per copy.

But don't pin this on V3: per 3.2 both its moments are bf16: 4+2+2 = 8 bytes, 4.9 TiB per copy, a third below the classic count. Whatever saves optimizer state saves checkpoint size too.

Two engineering facts follow:

  • Why checkpoints are so big and slow to save. They store mostly the optimizer; the model is only a third.
  • Why released weights are so much smaller than a checkpoint. A release needs only the 2-byte inference weights; the checkpoint's 12 bytes are all for training: one to six.

⛔ These 12 bytes aren't enough. Miss any of three more things and “resume” becomes “restart.”

  • ① Step count: the learning rate, β₂ and weight decay may all be functions of the step (3.5, 3.6).
  • ② Data-reader position: easiest to miss, hardest to spot: resuming retrains the same batches while the loss curve looks perfectly normal.
  • ③ RNG state: needed for dropout and data shuffling.

The “roll back + skip data” rescue in §6.2 depends on ① and ②. Without the data position, you can't say which batches to skip.

A real saving: the optimizer part needn't live on the accelerator. DeepSeek-V3 keeps an exponential moving average of the weights in CPU memory, updated async each step (no HBM, no training time), to preview quality after LR decay. 📌 arXiv 2412.19437 §3.2.3.

3.8 LoRA: the training most people actually do

So far we trained from scratch. Most people fine-tune someone else's trained model.

No new concepts: the same 16-byte budget, redone for a different algorithm.

The authors' reasoning first, or the “skinny matrices” look like a mere trick

The pain: you can't store a 175B copy per customer.

The abstract opens with it: fully fine-tuning GPT-3 175B means a separate 175B-parameter instance per downstream task, “prohibitively expensive.”

⭐ The pain is in deployment, not in training. LoRA was built for “one base, hundreds of small add-ons”; saving training memory is a bonus.

Then the observation that prompted it.

Earlier work found that large models have huge parameter counts but a far lower effective dimension: the parameters sit in a thin subspace.

⭐ LoRA's leap of faith went one step further: if the model is low-dimensional, is the change from fine-tuning low-dimensional too?

A hypothesis, not a theorem. If it holds, the method writes itself: a low-rank change doesn't need a full-rank matrix; two skinny matrices multiplied suffice.

⭐ The shape of the reasoning: they didn't prove the change is low-rank. They built on the hypothesis, then measured it (the paper's “empirical investigation into rank-deficiency in language model adaptation”). Bet first, verify second.

📌 Hu et al., LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models, arXiv 2106.09685. The abstract: 10,000× fewer trainable parameters, 3× less GPU memory, and “unlike adapters, no additional inference latency.” That last point is how it beat earlier methods.

📌 The method in one sentence: freeze the base and attach a pair of skinny matrices beside it.

The 4096 × 4096 matrix stays frozen. Add a 4096 × 16 and a 16 × 4096; train only those.

The key is the 16: 2 × 4096 × 16 values, just 0.8% of the original.

What happens to the three budgets

BudgetFull fine-tuningLoRASaved?
Resident
weights + grads + optimizer		 16 B × all params 2 B × all (frozen, read-only)
+ 16 B × the 0.1%		 Biggest saving
Compute3× (fwd 1 + bwd 2) ≈ 2×A third
Activationswhole chain still whole chainBarely

Row one at 7B: dramatic. (Llama-2-7B class: 32 layers, hidden 4,096; 32 × 2 sites (Q, V) × 2 matrices (A, B) × 4,096 × 16 = 8,388,608.)

  • Full fine-tuning: 6.74e9 × 16 B = 100.4 GiB.
  • LoRA (a pair on Q and on V per layer, rank 16): frozen base 12.55 GiB + adapter 0.125 GiB = 12.68 GiB.

A 7.9× difference, from an adapter of only 8.39M parameters, 0.124% of the model.

Why so large: 14 of the 16 bytes (gradient + master weight + m + v) serve only updated parameters. A frozen one keeps just its 2-byte weight, as at inference.

Row two, “3× → 2×,” comes from 1.3.

Per 1.3 (① is forward), backward costs two matmuls: ② the weight gradient (for the optimizer), ③ the input gradient (passed down).

Frozen layers skip ② entirely: their weights never change, so nobody needs it.

Forward (1) plus ③ (1) gives about 2×, not 3×.

Don't confuse the reverse: tuning just the last layer saves ③ (nothing flows back). LoRA has adapters in every layer, so ③ remains; it saves ②.

Row three: most misunderstood, most valuable.

“Training 0.1% of parameters = light training”? Not in memory.

Adapters sit on every layer. The first layer's adapter needs a gradient, which only flows back from the loss (1.5). So the whole chain's activations stay.

After LoRA, activations are often the largest item, so it still needs recomputation (Section 2). The two stack; neither replaces the other.

Strictly, activations shrink a little, depending on where adapters sit. Rarely spelled out:

  • A fully frozen linear layer: its input can go: only ② in 1.3 (weight gradient) needs it, and ② is skipped.
  • An adapter pins the input back: A reads the same input, and A's gradient needs it.

Counterintuitive corollary: the more adapters, the less activation memory saved. “Q and V only” saves a little: none of the three big MLP matrices has one. “More adapters work better” costs activations, not parameters.

Nonlinear ops' inputs still stay, so the total shrinks a little, not by an order of magnitude. Derived from 1.3's two matmuls; not measured.

⭐⭐⭐ Wrap-up: LoRA changes how many parameters carry 16 bytes, not that backward traverses the whole network. The parameter side shrinks; the chain doesn't: it comes from backprop, not from how many parameters you train.

Section 4

The bill goes to Topic 5 (not covered here)

A bridge to Topic 5. Rank the items by size: ZeRO's three stages follow that order.

A Topic 5 preview, not one of our three things. Three sentences; details collapsed below.

What training needs, by size:

Optimizer state (12 B/param) > weights = gradients (2 B each) > activations (batch-dependent)

  • When it doesn't fit, shard in this order: largest, least-used first.
  • That is ZeRO's three stages: optimizer state, then gradients, weights last.
  • How, onto whom, at what communication cost: Topic 5's job.

Takeaway: parallelism isn't invented; this bill's size ranking forces it.

The bill: the four items' sizes, how ZeRO's stages follow, what each other technique shards Topic 5 preview, not required

4.1 First, rank the bill by size

Put the items from the last three sections side by side and rank them by size. That ranking is this whole section.

Item/param671BShareWhat it isWhen used
Optimizer state12 B7.32 TiB75%fp32 master 4, moments m 4, v 4Once, at the update instant
Weights2 B1.22 TiB12.5%bf16 copy; both passes use itRead by every layer
Gradients2 B1.22 TiB12.5%bf16, shaped like the weightsWritten in backward; dropped after update
Resident total16 B9.76 TiB100%⭐ Independent of batch and seq. length: the model fixes it.
Activations—By batch—Saved for backward (1.6)⛔ Only one you control; only one that can outgrow the rest

The first three rows are bytes per parameter × parameter count, so the ratio is always 12 : 2 : 2, whatever the model or device count.

Optimizer state alone is 75% of the resident total, yet the only one neither pass uses: 3.1 showed it is read and written once, at the update instant.

⛔ The fourth row is different: it is the only one you control.

The first three follow the parameter count; no choice. Activations follow the tokens live at once this step: micro-batch × grad accum × DP degree × seq. length, four knobs multiplied.

So “which item is largest” is a property of the training configuration, not of the model. Push the batch far enough and the fourth row passes the first; 5.1 finds the crossover.

Remember this order: next, ZeRO works down it one stage at a time.

4.2 ZeRO's three stages follow exactly this order

No need to memorize ZeRO's stages: reverse the order above and you've derived them.

One rule sets the order: shard the largest, least-used item first.

  • ZeRO-1 shards optimizer state. The largest, used only once, at the update, so sharding it adds almost no communication. Best value.
  • ZeRO-2 then shards gradients. Weight-sized, but they can stay scattered until backward finishes.
  • ZeRO-3 (≈ FSDP) shards the parameters last. Every layer's forward needs them, so once sharded each layer must all-gather them first: the most communication of the three.

So the order is no historical accident: it falls out of size and frequency of use.

📌 Source: Rajbhandari et al., “ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models,” arXiv 1910.02054. Section 3's “16 bytes per parameter” comes from it too: one paper gave both the bill and how to split it.

4.3 Same bill: what each other technique shards

Place the other techniques you keep hearing about on this bill and each one's place becomes obvious:

  • Recomputation (Section 2)—targets activations.
  • offload—targets whatever is not needed right now, slicing by stretch of time, not by item.
  • CP (context parallelism)—shards activations that grow with seq. length, overtaking optimizer state at long context.

⭐⭐⭐ These are not “a few optimization tricks” but countermeasures for four different columns of the same bill. All of Topic 5 is about what the sharding itself costs.

Section 5

All three, on a machine at hand

All correct, but all at 671B parameters and TiB scale, with no reference point. Now shrink it to a model you can work out yourself.

Forward (Topic 1), backward and update in one table. The useful question isn't “how much” but “when is the peak?”

Full step bill: four-item total, why 6ND underestimates, when it peaks “Does it fit?”: Topic 5 preview, optional

5.1 Memory: four items added

Four sections, four separate accounts; now add them up. Global totals, no per-device split (next lecture's job).

📌 The resident block fits in your head:

671e9 params × 16 bytes ÷ 1024⁴ = 9.76 TiB. Broken down: weights 1.22 + gradients 1.22 + optimizer state 7.32.

For scale: at 80 GiB per device, this block alone needs 125 devices, before activations or any redundancy. The activation peak below assumes full recompute; per 2.4, V3 itself recomputes selectively (RMSNorm + MLA up-projections). Different bases: full is a clean floor; reality runs higher. (80 GiB: just a round base, not a product. Topic 1 uses v7's 94.74 GiB/device: about 105 devices. Same TiB, other divisor.)

Of these three, only the optimizer state's 7.32 TiB is pure overhead: no part in forward or backward, used once at the end of each step.

Follow that number one step further: a surprise.

The resident 9.76 TiB is fixed, whatever the sequences. How large must activations grow to catch up?

About 8.08M tokens. At this lecture's 4K baseline, about 1,973 sequences. (Full recomputation: one 4K sequence peaks at 5.07 GiB; one 128K sequence (context extension), 162.14 GiB: about 62 sequences, same token count.)

Stop: this number is easy to plug in wrong. I did, in one draft.

3.5 says V3's global batch starts at 3,072 sequences of 4K (= 12.58M tokens) and later ramps to 15,360. That looks far past the 8.08M crossover.

Global batch won't do: the crossover counts what's live at once.

global batch = DP degree × micro-batch × grad-accum K × seq length, and the K slices never coexist (point ④, 1.8). Only the first two are live at once, as in panel Ⓑ.

A safe upper bound: V3 used 2,048 devices with PP16 × EP64. Most generous DP, 2048 ÷ 16 = 128-way, micro-batch 1: only 128 sequences = 520K tokens live at once, under a fourteenth of the crossover.

So “activations overtake optimizer state from step one” is false: withdrawn. On V3's own config, 3.1's “the largest block is optimizer state” still holds.

This passage once said “V3 passes the crossover 1.7× from step one, 8.5× late in training” (vs. the old 7.37M-token crossover; today's 8.08M gives 1.56× and 7.8×), as if the example overturned the first answer. That treated global batch as live at once. Yet the figure was right all along: Ⓑ reads “live at once = DP degree × micro-batch.” Rule: when figure and text state one quantity, first check they share a definition. Figure right, text wrong, both self-consistent: no alarm.

One premise that's easy to skip: memory doesn't care how those 8.08M tokens are made up.

  • About 1,973 sequences of 4K or about 62 of 128K: for memory, the same.
  • Why: the activation bill has no S² term: the attention score matrix never lands in memory (the second caveat in 1.7). Every remaining item is “one per token,” so only total tokens count.

⛔ But compute doesn't.

The same 8.08M tokens as long sequences or as short ones need very different compute: attention grows with S², and it is on the compute bill, not the memory bill.

So the sequence-length knob behaves differently on the two bills: memory only sees the total; compute also sees the split. Hence 5.2's “6ND badly underestimates.”

The premise: all this assumes FlashAttention. A naive version storing the score matrix puts S² back on the memory bill; none of the above holds.

5.2 Compute: 6ND badly underestimates long context

The usual training-compute estimate is 6ND: about 6 FLOPs per parameter per token (2 forward, 4 backward: the 1 + 2 from Section 1).

Plugging in (for MoE, active parameters, not total): 6 × 37e9 × 131,072 ≈ 29.1 PFLOP for one 128K sequence.

⛔ But at 128K this number is badly wrong.

6ND counts weight multiplications. The attention steps QKᵀ and AV involve no weights, so the formula ignores them.

Appendix 7.2 puts attention at 82.1% of a layer's forward compute at 128K, so 6ND captures only the remaining 17.9%.

So real compute exceeds 6ND by five to six times: the 29.1 PFLOP is actually close to 160 PFLOP.

This multiplier is derived from the 82.1% (1 ÷ 0.179), our own per-op estimate: magnitude only. Remember not the multiplier but when the formula misleads: long sequences.

Conversely, 6ND works very well for short sequences. At GPT-3's 2,048, attention is just over 1%, negligible. Same lesson: the formula isn't wrong; the premise changed.

5.3 Peak: first ask “the peak of what”

Section 1's mountain figure said the peak is at the end of forward. That holds only for activations.

Draw all four items on one timeline (the figure above) and different items peak at different moments.

Generalized, a rule you can use anywhere:

when you stack curves of different shapes, the peak of the sum need not fall on any single curve's peak. Always ask “crowded with what” along with “when is it most crowded.”

📌 In practice: debugging an OOM, “the peak is xx GiB” is useless; you need which item is largest then. Large activations: recompute or add CP. Large optimizer state: ZeRO. Mix them up and neither helps.

5.4 One step of a 125M-parameter model

The three things on this machine:

  • ① How the loss is computed: 8,192 positions, one −ln p each, averaged. At init it is ln(vocab), 1.0's yardstick; a smaller vocabulary starts a bit lower.
  • ② How many derivatives one number becomes: 125M, for “two more forward passes,” not 125M (1.1).
  • ③ How big a step to take: Adam keeps two moving averages for every parameter: 8 of the 12 bytes. The other 4, fp32 master weights, come from mixed precision, not Adam (3.1).

Below, ③ becomes a number you can check.

📌 Setup: a 125M-parameter model, one device, batch 8 × sequence 1,024.

12 layers, width 768, MLP 3,072: row one of GPT-3's Table 2.1 (top row of 3.5's table).

Step 1 · The resident block

The same 16 bytes as in 3.1:

ItemPer param125M params
bf16 weights2 B0.23 GiB
bf16 gradients2 B0.23 GiB
Optimizer state (fp32 master weights + m + v)12 B1.40 GiB
Subtotal16 B1.86 GiB

First checkable conclusion: weights are 0.23 GiB, training takes 1.86 GiB, eight times more, all of it training-only.

Step 2 · The activations

What each token leaves per layer, item by item (width 768):

Saved tensorWidth
Outputs of the two norms2 × 768 = 1,536
Q / K / V3 × 768 = 2,304
Attention output768
MLP layer-1 output3,072
Activation output3,072
MLP layer-2 output768
Per layer11,520 values = 22.5 KiB (bf16)

× 12 layers = 270 KiB per token. × 8,192 tokens = 2.11 GiB.

⛔ Something surprising happened.

Activations 2.11 GiB > resident 1.86 GiB. At only 125M parameters, activations exceed weights, gradients and optimizer state combined.

No long context: sequence 1,024, batch 8. Recomputation isn't just for big models.

Step 3 · With recomputation

As in 2.2: each layer keeps its input (width 768), plus all of the layer being recomputed.

0.32 GiB: down from 2.11, 6.7× less, for compute 3× → 4×.

The 0.32 GiB has a deliberate omission checkers will hit.

It counts the 12 layers only, not the final logits. GPT-3 reuses GPT-2's BPE vocabulary, about 50.3K:

8,192 tokens × 50,257 × 2 B = 0.77 GiB, 2.4× the 0.32 GiB.

Materialize all logits at once, and the largest item here is neither weights nor activations but the vocabulary score table. Real code computes the loss in chunks, so it's left out (1.7). An accounting choice; the logits still exist.

📌 50.3K, in two hops: GPT-3 paper §2.1: “We use the same model and architecture as GPT-2, including the modified initialization, pre-normalization, and reversible tokenization described therein,” so GPT-2's BPE: 50,257. GPT-3 never prints it. 30K or 60K changes nothing.

Recompute offRecompute on
Resident1.86 GiB1.86 GiB
Activations2.11 GiB0.32 GiB
Total3.97 GiB2.18 GiB
Compute3×4× (+33%)

This is the training loop on your laptop.

  • The 16-byte budget (3.1): gives the 1.86 GiB.
  • Activations grow with total tokens (5.1, this section): the 2.11 GiB's only variable is the 8,192 tokens.
  • Trading compute for memory (2.2): pay 33% more, save 6.7×.

“Pay 33%” matches 671B, but “save 6.7×” is 3× smaller than its 20.5×.

An earlier draft said “the ratios are almost the same as for 671B.” Far from it. Why is the more valuable part.

Why does the same “full recomputation” save 6.7× here and 20.5× there?

Write it as a formula. Let r = one layer's activations ÷ its input, L = layers:

Saving = r ÷ (1 + r/L)

Numerator r: how much a layer holds; fatter layers save more.
Denominator term: the layer being recomputed, amortized over layers; more layers, less impact.

r = activations ÷ inputL = layersSaving
125M small model15 (11,520 ÷ 768)126.7
The rows define r a bit differently: the small model counts only the norms' outputs; V3 (1.7's table) adds their inputs (= residual input). With inputs, small-model r = 16, saving 6.9. Same magnitude and conclusion; strictly two rulers.
This cell once had a hand-typed “r ≈ 16, saving ≈ 7.1.” 16 was right; the formula gives 6.9, not 7.1. Telling: every other number here was script-computed; this one, hand-typed.
V3 671B31.7 (one MoE block ÷ 7,168)6120.5

The small model loses on both: r 2.1× smaller, L 5× smaller. The smaller saving is inevitable, not an error.

The large r is MoE's: in 1.7's table, expert outputs and SwiGLU intermediates are each stored nine times. A fuller layer saves more. MoE saves on parameters, costs on activations, and therefore pays off especially on recomputation. One design, three bills, three directions.

For V3 the formula gives 20.8 vs. 20.5 measured: slightly lower, as the 3 dense layers are thinner than MoE. An order of magnitude, not exact.

Only three things are truly scale-independent.

  • Pay 33% more. It depends only on “forward twice, not once,” not model size or sequence length.
  • 16 bytes per parameter. 125M or 671B, the breakdown is identical (3.1).
  • Activations count only total tokens. 8,192 tokens or 8.08M, same rule.

The saving factor is not on this list. It follows r and L: new architecture, new math. Criterion ③ again: separate what changes from what doesn't.

Same three caveats as 1.7's table: ① derived op by op; fusion shrinks them; read as magnitudes; ② excludes the attention score matrix (FlashAttention assumed), temp, fragmentation and comm buffers; ③ “0.32 GiB” assumes a checkpoint every layer, not always the leanest density (2.2 Ⓒ).

What goes to Topic 5 Handoff to parallelism

5.5 What this bill hands to the next lecture

Topic 1 ended the forward pass with “it doesn't fit.” With the bill complete, that becomes specific: “each of the four items doesn't fit, and each has its own remedy.”

Four items, four remedies:

  • Optimizer state (largest, least used) → shard (ZeRO-1)
  • Gradients (weight-sized; scattered till backward ends) → shard (ZeRO-2)
  • Weights (used by all layers) → shard last (ZeRO-3 / FSDP): costliest comms
  • Activations (∝ batch × seq. length) → recompute, or shard by seq. (CP)

⭐⭐⭐ Three of four lines say one word: shard. That is all of Topic 5: sharding has its own cost, to be accounted for too.

Section 6

Not blowing up: when the loss spikes, and how to prevent it

So far, accounting. It can't answer the most common question on a real run: “The loss just shot up. Now what?”

6.0 Naming the failure modes

We've met five failure modes across five sections, each under its own name. Side by side: on a real run, the hard part is diagnosis, not the fix.

NameSymptomRoot cause ConfirmRemedy
Exploding gradients Loss NaN/Inf, or grad norm jumps decades in one step Local derivatives stay above 1; 61 layers compound them expo­nentially (1.4) Global grad norm per step: decade jumps? Clipping (6.4) · Pre-LN (6.5)
Vanishing gradients Input-side layers barely move, as if just initialized Same chain, local derivatives below 1 Per-layer grad norm: decays with depth? Pre-LN and init (6.5)
Rounded-away updates
(“won't train”)		 Loss flat despite nonzero gradient; fp32 master weights fix it at once Per-step relative change below mantissa resolution (about 1/256 for bf16) Compare update RMS ÷ param RMS with 1/256 fp32 master weights (3.2)
Step-size diver­gence Loss climbs, or oscillates with growing amplitude η exceeds 2 ÷ sharpest curvature: steps overshoot, amplified along it Halve η and rerun: instantly fine means this LR ceiling and warmup (3.3b · 3.5)
Loss spike
(instability)		 Sudden spike in smooth training; heals or collapses Not bad data: there's an ablation (6.2) Rerun same batches: spike again? This section, 6.1⁠–⁠6.6

Rows one and two: one chain of products, two directions.

Per 1.4, a parameter's gradient is 61 local derivatives multiplied. Above 1 on average, it grows exponentially; below 1, it decays. So the fixes are one family: keep each local derivative near 1, as 6.5's structural fixes do.

The middle rows (rounding, divergence) are both called “won't train”, with opposite remedies: bigger steps or more precision vs. smaller steps. Confusing them hurts.

6.1 First, a real case

📏 First, the yardstick from 1.0.

“Blew up” is a feeling; we want judgment. In numbers:

  • Late pretraining, loss hovers around 2: normal.
  • A jump to 6: perplexity 7 → 400. Back to “knows only word frequencies”, but still knows the words.
  • A jump to 11.8, ln 129,280: everything forgotten, uniform guessing.

So spike height tells whether the run can be saved. A jump to 6 usually clears by rolling back a few dozen steps; a jump to ln V wastes that stretch.

⛔ PaLM 540B's loss spiked roughly 20 times.

With gradient clipping on. The spikes came at highly irregular times, sometimes late, and never in the smaller models.

📌 arXiv 2204.02311 §5.1. “Roughly 20 times” and “despite the fact that gradient clipping was enabled” are verbatim.

Scale effect: fine when small isn't safe when large. Like “don't copy across scales” in 2.6, but what breaks is training itself, not the payoff.

6.2 The surprising ablation: not bad data

First instinct: bad batch. PaLM tested it cleanly:

They replayed the batches around the spike from an earlier checkpoint. No spike.

Spikes aren't “bad data”: these batches collide with that parameter state.

Same data, other moment: nothing.

Hence their crude fix works: roll back to a checkpoint ~100 steps before the spike, skip those 200–500 batches, resume. It doesn't recur.

Not “fixed”: “worked around”. Given the cost, they “were not able to determine a principled strategy to mitigate these spikes”. Still open.

6.3 The hard part: stable without losing quality

A tiny learning rate or very tight clipping stops spikes. All cost model quality.
