ST-MoE measured this. Same config, different seeds: how many runs finish, at what quality:

MethodStabilityQuality ↑Verdict
Baseline4 / 6−1.7552 of 6 runs diverged
This is log-likelihood, not loss: negative, and higher is better (−1.755 beats −4.206). On the 1.0 yardstick: loss 1.755 vs. 4.206, perplexity 5.8 vs. 67. Not the same quantity as loss.
Tighter update clipping (0.1)3 / 3−4.206 Stable, but quality wrecked
router z-loss3 / 3−1.741 Stable, slightly better

The middle row is the point: “stable 3/3” looks perfect, bought with quality. Judge stability techniques on both columns.

Two caveats against over-reading it.

  • Different denominators. Baseline: 6 seeds; each technique: 3 seeds. “4/6” vs. “3/3” is not like-for-like. Three runs are far too few for “guaranteed stable”.
  • The setup was deliberately chosen. Per the authors, small models rarely go unstable; large ones are too costly for enough seeds. So: a config diverging about one run in three, on multilingual data, found to worsen instability, so slightly smaller models suffice.

Not a flaw: good design. To study a rare failure, make it common first. But remember: the failure rate was dialed up.

📌 arXiv 2202.08906 (ST-MoE), Table 4. Its heading: “Many methods stabilize sparse models, but at the expense of worse quality.”

6.4 Fix 1 (numerics): cap what grows too large

z-loss: rein in pre-softmax logits

Simple: a loss term penalizing the squared log of the softmax normalizer. It pushes log Z toward 0, keeping logits small.

Two places, both used:

  • On the output softmax — PaLM uses 10⁻⁴ · log²Z, which increases training stability per the paper.
  • On the MoE router — the router z-loss above. Near-mandatory for MoE: routing is a softmax too, and if its logits blow up, routing swings wildly.

Why z-loss is cheap insurance: per ST-MoE, logits feed an exponential, extremely sensitive to input error. A smaller input range directly cuts that risk, and the model doesn't need the dynamic range.

Gradient clipping: a seatbelt, not a knob

Clip by global norm: treat all gradients as one vector; if its norm exceeds the threshold, scale it down. 1.0 is usual (PaLM, DeepSeek-V3: both 1.0).

But recall 6.1: PaLM spiked 20 times with clipping on. Clipping stops a one-step explosion, not parameters already drifted somewhere bad.

6.5 Fix 2 (structure): hard to blow up by design

Where the norm goes, which settles 3.5's open question

First, split a layer into three parts to see the difference. A layer is two parallel paths. The trunk carries x unchanged. The branch runs x through attention or the MLP for a correction F(x). They merge into x + F(x): 1.4's residual.

Normalization, part three, must sit on one of these paths. Post-LN and Pre-LN differ only in where.

Two placements

Post-LN xt+1 = Norm( xt + F(xt) )
Merge, then Norm the whole trunk, every layer.

Pre-LN xt+1 = xt + F( Norm(xt) )
Norm moves into the branch. The trunk is untouched, straight to the top.

Neither wins yet. But it's not a matter of style.

A 2020 paper proved it, with a conclusion tied to 3.5:

At init, Post-LN has large gradients near the output, so a large learning rate is bound to be unstable; warmup holds that in check.
Pre-LN's gradients are well-behaved at init, so the paper says Pre-LN can drop warmup.

Recall 3.5's table, third row. Its “precondition” reads “significant vanishing gradients (i.e., Post-LN)”: this exponential decay.
So warmup doesn't have “competing explanations”: the 2020 paper explains why it was once indispensable; 3.5's paper, why it's still around. Different questions.

📌 arXiv 2002.04745 (ICML 2020), via mean-field theory.

That says Post-LN gradients are bad, not why. The mechanism is one sentence and answers a sharper question: if it's bad, why keep it?

⛔ Post-LN is xt+1 = Norm(xt + Ft(xt)).

At init, x and F(x) are roughly independent random vectors, each of variance 1, so their sum has variance 2. Norm pulls it back to 1: effectively ÷ √2.

Recursing, the coefficient of input x₀ in layer l's output is 2−l/2. The residual “shortcut” shrinks exponentially, most near the input.

Su Jianlin's verdict, harsh but well founded: “In a Post Norm BERT model, LN not only fails to mitigate vanishing gradients; it is one of the ‘culprits’ behind them.”

So why not remove it? Without it, x + F(x) has variance 2, growing with each residual. The question is “where”, not “whether”: Pre-LN uses x + F(Norm(x)) plus one final Norm, so all residual branches weigh equally and the decay is gone.

Most counterintuitive: elsewhere, this “bug” is a feature.

Fine-tuning should adjust parameters near the output first and barely move those near the input, to preserve what pretraining learned. Vanishing gradients mean “closer to the input, weaker effect on the output”: exactly what fine-tuning wants.

So pretrained Post-LN models often fine-tune better than Pre-LN. That's the figure's two halves.

📌 Source and disclaimer per 3.5 (Su Jianlin, kexue.fm/archives/8747). It once said “see the footnote in 3.4”, wrongly: that footnote cites another post by the same author (archives/11267, on update RMS 0.2).

Of the three warmup explanations in 3.5, this confirms one precondition. The third, “hold back later layers until earlier ones catch up,” relies on this exponential decay. Pre-LN lacks it, so that explanation doesn't apply.

QK-norm: runaway attention scores

At around 8B parameters, ViT diverged within a few thousand steps: attention logits grew huge, so post-softmax weights collapsed to near one-hot (near-zero entropy).

The fix: LayerNorm Q and K before the dot product. Hence QK-norm, now standard in many large models.

📌 arXiv 2302.05442 (ViT-22B) §2. QK-norm was not invented by ViT-22B. The paper says “we adopt the approach of Gilmer et al. (2023)”. ViT-22B applied it at 22B parameters, with a comparison figure: hence the citation. Again a failure that only appears at scale, as in 6.1.

Initialization: brief, but don't skip it

With every residual branch initialized at one scale, the signal grows with depth. Standard practice: scale residual-branch init down with depth. It won't prevent spikes, but sets your starting point.

6.6 Two common misconceptions

❓ “Does bf16 need loss scaling?” No.

In short: same 16 bits, split differently. fp16 favors “fine resolution”; bf16 favors “reaching tiny values”. fp16's problem isn't coarseness; it can't go low enough: a small gradient becomes exactly 0, and that parameter gets no signal that step. Loss scaling is simple: shift values up, off the floor.

Loss scaling was an fp16-era necessity: fp16 has only 5 exponent bits, so small gradients underflow to 0. Scale the loss up before backprop, down before the update.
bf16 has fp32's 8 exponent bits: same range, less mantissa. No underflow, no loss scaling.

Pairs with 3.2: bf16 buys “enough range, poor precision”: the danger is accumulation, not underflow.

❓ “Should training be reproducible?” It can be, and it pays.

PaLM was bitwise reproducible: restart from any checkpoint and every later step matches the original run exactly.

It takes a deterministic compute framework and a deterministic data pipeline: the batch depends only on the step, not on process count or resumes.

6.2's “roll back + skip data” needs this. Otherwise, which batches to skip?

📌 Also from arXiv 2204.02311.

6.7 Takeaway: four rules

Back to the start.

Section 0: training uses one number to decide which way each of 671B parameters moves.

Every part is now explained:

  • That number — −ln p, the model's surprise at the right answer. From 11.77 (uniform guessing) to around 2. (1.0)
  • How one number becomes 671B derivatives — many in, few out, so going backward from the output is cheapest. 671B forward passes become one backward pass. (1.5)
  • How big a step to take — direction is computed; step size isn't. Fifty years of optimizers fight that unanswerable question. (3.3b)

All that accounting (3× compute, undroppable intermediates, 16 B/param) just moves it from 11.8 to 2.

Near 2, each 0.01 is expensive, paid with the whole bill you just worked out.

Dozens of numbers. Not what we want you to keep.

  • ① High precision or not compares two numbers: “this quantity's relative change per step” vs. “the smallest step the mantissa resolves”. Adjacent bf16 values differ by 1/128 (7 mantissa bits, 2⁻⁷), so the “added vs. rounded away” threshold is half that, about 1/256.
    Both right, different quantities: 1/128 is the grid spacing (the 0.0078125 in Ⓑ of 3.2's precision figure); 1/256 is the rounding threshold (under half a step, nothing changes). Use the latter.
    Moving averages forget each step, so they move; master weights sum 100K steps of a few thousandths each, so they can't. (3.2)
  • ② Recompute or not: “FLOPs paid per byte saved”. For a linear layer, the input width; for attention, linear in sequence length. Different slopes, so they cross. (2.3)
  • ③ If two quantities grow at different rates in one variable, and the faster one starts lower, their ranking must flip somewhere. So any “A beats B” needs the range where it holds; without it, the ranking is meaningless.
    The underlined condition was added on 2026-09-20; without it the rule is wrong. If the faster one also starts higher, the lines never cross on the positive axis; the ranking never changes. Our example (2.4, crossing at S ≈ 13,107) is the “slower one starts higher” case, so it held. A rule always holds on its own example, where it's hardest to falsify.
    Fixed, it's more useful: to predict a flip, check which grows faster and which starts lower.
    Here it flipped several times, each in a different variable: sequence length (2.4), model scale (6.1, this section), and one switch whose payoff even changes sign across scales (2.6).
  • ④ Judge stability techniques on “stable?” and “quality lost?”. On the first alone, a zero learning rate is optimal. (6.3, this section)

⭐⭐⭐ Numbers go stale. These four rules won't.

Deliberately, none of our own measurements here: all four come from papers, each checked at the source. Why (§7): the lecture has many self-derived numbers; stability shouldn't add more.

Two rows where our criteria are the API names.

  • dots_with_no_batch_dims_saveable: “save matmul outputs.” Why matmuls? Each byte they save costs the most FLOPs to recompute: the closed form in 2.3.
  • ddp.no_sync(): no_sync() switches off stage ② entirely. No communication while accumulating; one sync at the end. Saving communication is this API's purpose, not a side effect of accumulation.
  • core_attn is Megatron's default once selective is on (not “on by default”: recompute_granularity defaults to None), and the source warns it's unneeded with fused attention. Yet by 2.4, at long context it is the last thing to recompute. Defaults have a vintage (2.5). Not a contradiction: 2.2's “recomputation is on by default in large-model training” is industry practice; recompute_granularity = None is the factory setting. Different “defaults.”

One option we skip: PyTorch's CheckpointPolicy has six enum values, not two: {MUST,PREFER}_SAVE, {MUST,PREFER}_RECOMPUTE, {MUST,PREFER}_CPU_OFFLOAD.
Each activation is a choice of three: keep in HBM / recompute / offload to CPU and back. We cover the first two. The third buys HBM with PCIe bandwidth instead of compute: same trade, different currency.
MUST vs. PREFER, docs: “Use MUST_* over PREFER_* to indicate that the policy should not be overridden by other subsystems like torch.compile.”

So the table is a reverse check: if your criterion doesn't match the options, your criterion is likely wrong, or the default stale.

This table goes stale first:

Every name was grepped live from each main branch in September 2026, not from memory. Frameworks rename often.

Rule: when you give a name, give the file it lives in. Otherwise a rename makes it misleading, and nothing errors.

NumberDerivationWeak points
Activations 104.11 GiB → recom­puted peak 5.07 GiB (4K) Op by op (1.7's two tables). Inputs: V3's config + the reference MLA forward Op fusion; does MoE dispatch really make nine copies?
Attention = 82.1% of a layer's compute Causal-halved. We once said Topic 1's “independent” 81.8% agreed. Wrong; retracted. Same numerator (one formula, S²·H·(dqk+dv), one config, same halving); only denominators differ: whole model incl. lm_head (Topic 1) vs. one layer's active params. The 0.463% gap = lm_head dilution: 81.8 ÷ (1−0.00463) = 82.18. Convention (halved?); head dims. Self-check, not an external anchor: same source, must agree. No third-party data yet
Crossover S ≈ 13,107 1.25·S = 16,384 (o_proj input = 128 heads × 128); 1.25 = V3 head dims 192/128, causal-halved. Earlier: d_model 7,168 → 5,734. “Widest linear = d_model” fails for MLA Another layer moves it. Not an engineering threshold
6ND is 5–6× too low Back-derived from the 82.1% above (1 ÷ 0.179) Inherits the 82.1%'s doubt; no third-party check yet
9.76 TiB resident block · crossover at ~1,973 4K sequences 671e9 × 16 B ÷ 1024⁴ ÷ 5.07 GiB peak. Peak must include the layer being recomputed; checkpoints alone give 2,997 (52% high). Build-time assert 16 B is the classic convention; V3 isn't set up that way (3.2)

Why this section exists.

Both kinds look identical (a few digits and a unit), and readers copy them together.

⭐⭐⭐ Rule: a self-derived number must come with its derivation, or it is posing as a fact.

📌 A method, with a counterexample here: an isolated estimate is unverifiable; one matching an “external” anchor checks the whole formula. Our 82.1% has no anchor: as retracted, it shares a source with Topic 1's 81.8%, so had to agree. “They agree” counts only if paths are truly independent.
